summary: The respondent assessee was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 66, 1966 67 and 1967 68 (the respective valuation dates being March 31, 1965 and March 31. 1967). The Wealth Tax Officer included a sum of Rs. 1,50,000/- on accrual basis (though not realised) on the outstandings of the money lending business, the accounts of the assessee being maintained on cash basis basis. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected the claim of the respondent assessee that accrued interest was liable to be included in the wealth tax assessments of the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the accrued interest could not be included within the wealth Tax assessment of the Income Tax Officer because the assets were not circumscribed by any consideration of the particular system of accounting adopted by the assessee. HELD: The expression "net wealth" in section 2(1) (2) indicates that it refers to the last day of the previous year as defined under the Income tax Act, if an assessment is made in pursuance of section 19A, the valuation date shall be the same valuation date as would have been adopted in respect of the net wealth of the deceased if he were alive. [310 G] The expression 'net wealth' which speaks of "the aggregate value" of all the assets belonging to the assessee on the valuation day is not restricted by any considerations of the specific system of accountancy adopted by it. It is immaterial whether the assessee employs one system of Accounting or another. Where the asset is an asset other than cash, its value is determined pursuant to sub section (I) of s.7 as the estimated price, which, in the opinion of the Wealth Tax officer, the asset would fetch if sold in the open market on the Valuation date. It was immaterial whether such assets were intended to be covered by the Wealth tax Act. That being so, the conclusion is inescapable that even though the accounts are maintained on Cash basis interest due on accrual base, though not realised, on the sale date, could not fall to be excluded in the net Wealth of the petitioner. [334 C] The principle underlying the scheme of the wealthtax Act is that the assets to be considered are not circumscribed either by anyconsideration of the relevant system of accounts adopted by him or by any other consideration of particular system. Where there are different previous years under the Wealthtax Act, the value is determination pursuant to subsection (I), of section 7 as the estimate of the value which, according to the WealthTax Officer, the assets would fetch, if sold, in open market On the valuation dates, the last date of the income tax "previous year" stop there. The method of accounting, mercantile or cash or hybrid is of no relevance for the purpose of determining the assets of the business of the company. [313 G] Commissioner of Wealth Tax vs Vysyaraju Badreenarayana Moorthy Raju (Orissa) (supra). The method adopted by a statutory provision is of little assistance to the Revenue and it is immaterial that whether the asset was an asset or not. Where, the assessee uses one system or another, it is irrelevant whether the entity employs one systems of accounting or another and it does not fall within the assets.

The respondent was a workman in the appellant company. He was dismissed from service on the ground that he had committed misconduct and was not found guilty of any misconduct. The respondent filed an application before the Central Administrative Tribunal for setting aside the order of dismissal. The Tribunal held that the punishment of dismissal should be maintained but set aside the penalty imposed by the disciplinary authority. The appellant company preferred a writ petition in this Court challenging the order passed by the Tribu nal on the grounds that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to interfere with the penalty if the conclusion of the Inquiry Officer or the Tribunal was based on evidence even if some of it is found to be irrelevant or extraneous to the matter. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court has no juris diction under Article 226 of the Constitution to interfere in a case where the Tribunal is satisfied that if some but not all of t he findings of the Tribunal were "unreasonable", the order cannot be sustained. [27F] 2.1 In the instant case, the Tribunal imposed a lesser penalty on the respond ent. The Court has not gone into the question whether the punishment imposed by th e disciplinary authority can be supported on any finding as to substantial misdemeanour for which the punishment can lawfully be imposed, it is not for the Court to consider whether that ground alone would have weighed with the authority in imposing the punishment. [28F] 3.2 The Tribunal has no jurisdiction if the findings of t his Inquiry Officer are based on the evidence even though some of them may be found to he irrelevant or irrelevant. If the inference that the penalty of dismissal from service imposed upon the appellant was too seve rred, it was not for thority to consider any finding on substantial misdemeanor for which t he punishment could lawfully be impose, it has no merits. [29F] 4. The order of the Tribun al imposing a lesser punishment on the appel lant cannot, therefore, be sustained.[30A B] 5. In Shankar Dass vs Union of India this Court set aside t he impugned order of penalty on t he ground that the imposition of the penalty was too harsh to the responde nt. [31F G] 6. The question whether a punishment of dismissing from service passed by an authority can he supported on some finding as regards substantial misdemeano f for which no penalty can lawfully been imposed, is not deter mined in this case since the respondent had already retired from service and his reinstatement in service was not challenged. [32F G; 33A] 7. The res pondent has failed to establish any misconduct or negligence on his part. If it is his case that he was not in fact the person convicted, it would be open to him to challenge the finding of the inquiry officer or the Tribuna nal. [33G H] 8. In the light of the principles to which we have call ed attention and in view of the aforesaid discussion, the ord er of the tribunal imposing a higher penalty on respondent cannot, however, be justified. [34F G].

The appellants were the legal representatives of the deceased plaintiff Inacio Martins who died pendente lite. He had filed a suit for declaration and an injunction to restrain the defendants from dispossessing him from the property known as 'Palmar Oiteral do Predio Aivao ' comprising seven lots of coconut grove situated at Caranzalem belonging to defendant No. 1. The first ground on which the High Court dismissed the suit was that the suit had been barred by the principle of res judicata in view of the dismissal of the former suit No. 157 of 1968 and hence, the subsequent suit was based on a distinct cause of action not found in the former case and hence the bar of Order 2 Rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure. The second suit based on the factum of tenancy was dismissed as the Trial Court came to the conclusion that the plaintiff was no more in possession of the property in respect of which he claimed to be a lessee. It would have been a different matter if in the previous suit the court had decided the question of status as lessee against the plaintiff, in which case, perhaps it could be argued that the second suit founded on the facts of the earlier suit was not maintainable. The High Court took the view that even after the Fifth Amendment came into force the plaintiff had not applied to the Mamlatdar for possession of his land within the period allowed by Section 18 of the Act and had, therefore, allowed the first defendant to become a deemed purchaser of the suit property on the strength of his tenancy. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The question which arose in the suit is whether defendant No 1 was a tenant or a deemed tenant. [1032C] 1.2 In such a situation the remedy may not be the one available in the case of a tenant other than a deemed tenants whose case is not governed by section 8(2) of Act. But in the cases of a deemed lessee who has been evicted from the land on or after 1st July, 1962 since a remedy has been provided under 1032 the Act, the Jurisdiction of the Civil Courts stands wholly barred by virtue of Section 58 (2) read section 58(2). [1033D] 2.1 In such an event the remedy would not be one available to the Civil Court to give any relief to the landlord by way of possession of agricultural land. If, on the other hand, the Mamlatdar rejects the plea raised under the Tenancy Act, he would be entitled to deal with the dispute on the footing that the defendant is a trespasser. [ 1034E] 2:2 In the instant case, the suit in question was based upon a distinct and cause of actions not found against the appellant. The jurisdiction of the civil court stands wholly excluded by virtue Section 58(1) of Bombay Tenancy Act. Therefore, the question which arises in the present suit was whether defendant 1 was tenant or deemed tenant was required to be decided by the Mamlatdar under section 7 read section 8 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948. [1004G] 2 :3 In such circumstances, the Civil court would not have been competent to pass any order for restoration of possession to the deemed tenant, because it would not otherwise be open to the civil Court to grant any relief in favour of the landlord.

The petitioners are carpenters in Government service. They claim that they are entitled to equal pay for equal work. The Corporation has adopted the minimum wages payable for similar work in the construction industry. The petitioners have been described as daily rated employees. The respondents contended that there were no regular employees of the petitioners ' establishment and, therefore, question of payment of salary admissible to them was not justified. Dismissing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The principle of equal pay is not one of the fundamental rights expressly guaranteed by our Constitution. It is important to emphasize that equal pay must depend upon the nature of work done, it cannot be judged by mere volume of work, there may be qualitative difference as regards reliability and responsibility. One cannot deny that often the difference is a matter of degree and that there is an element of value judgment by those who are charged with the administration in fixing the scales of pay and other conditions of service. [682B C] 1.2. The principles of equal wages cannot be invoked invariably in every kind of service particularly in the area of professional services. It will, therefore not be correct to provide two different pay scales in the same establishment on the basis of selection based on merit with due regard to experience and seniority. [782C D] 1.(a) The principle has to be read into Article 14 of the Constitution. In the instant case, the petitioners are employed by a company incorporated under the . By the general description of their job, one cannot come to the conclusion that every carpenter is equal to the other in the performance of his work. [667E] 1(b) The petitioners are engaged by a Company incorporated under section 617 of the Companies Act, 1956 and are being paid the minimum wage payable for identical work. They are being given the same pay as carpenter or craftsmen. The Court while rejecting the claim of the peti tioners, however, cannot direct the Corporation to apply the rates prescribed under exhibit P. 2 unless the Government makes it applicable to employees of Government service, the petitioner cannot enforce the right to "equal pay for Equal work" in every case of similar work. Nor can there be qualitative differences as regards quality and responsibility, nor can deny that sometimes the difference lies as regards value and responsibility.[667E F] 1:2. In view of the fact that equal wages for equal Work is a concomitant of Article 14, it is not possible to provide both different pay scale in the similar establishment and also to popular handicise and trade craftsman. [669G H] 2(a) There are no regular workmen of the petitioner ' establishment or, as such, the question of pay admissible to such workmen. The principal claim of these petitioners is fails and is rejected. [670E F G] 3(b). The principle for equal pay has not been invoked invariably In every case, there is a discrimination amongst the same set of employees by the same master in thesame establishment. It cannot be enforced. [671G H; 669A] 4(c) The principles laid down in Randhir Singh case are not applicable to the petitioners. The petition is dismissed.

The prosecution case was that on the date of occurrence, the deceased and his wife were staying in a house at about 9.30 p.m. The accused 1 to 3 were armed with deadly weapons and they were armed by their side. They were armed and were armed. On seeing them, the accused persons ran away from the place of occurrence. The deceased was taken to the hospital where he died on the way. The prosecution case further alleged that the accused had assaulted his wife and daughter in a car. The trial court convicted all the seven accused under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced them to undergo imprisonment for life under section 304 Part II read with Section 34 I P.C., and also to pay fine of Rs. 500/ each, and in default to suffer rigorous imprisonment for one year. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence awarded to accused 1 and 6 for the murder of Malan. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the retracted judicial confession of accused 5 could not be relied upon against him in view of the fact that he had been acquitted by the High Court of the charge of conspiracy under section 120B I. P. C.; (2) the confessional statement of accused 6 could not have been relied upon as a substantive piece of evidence; and (3) the confession of the accused 5 was inadmissible in evidence because it was retracted from his earlier statement recorded under section 164 Cr. P., which was not admissible in evidence. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The retracted judicial confessions of accused 4 could not therefore be relied on against accused 6 in view Of the fact, that accused 6 had been convicted by the trial court and sentenced to imprisonment for death under section 306 read with s 34 IP. C., and the confirmation of the conviction of accused 2, 3, 4, 5 and 7 by the Sessions Judge under section302 read with S 34 I I.A. could be sustained. [138 F] 2. The confession of Accused 6 was admissible in the trial proceedings as it was not retracted from the earlier statement made to him under section164 Cr.P., which had been recorded under Section 164 Cr P. P, and therefore, the retracted confession of an accused 5 cannot be relied against him. [139 G H] 3. The confessional statement made by accused 6 was inadmissible because it did not contain a recital that the deceased was in any way responsible for the commission of the offence. [140 C D] 4. The confessions of the two accused were admissible in law and could not, therefore, be relied only against accused 1, 6 and 7. [141 E F] 5. The statement made before the police under section 161 Cr. A. No. 348/79 was inadmissible as evidence because the confession was retracted by the accused.

The appellant 's father Sadagopalachar was a minor. He executed the will in favour of his mother and that he had put her signature on it when she was in sound disposing state of mind. The High Court held that the will was written in one room and Lakshmamma was lying in the adjoining room and it was after the will had been written that the statement of the scribe that the testator went into the adjoining door and read the will to her so that the appellant 'S case would be proved to be the last will and testament of Lakshmma. The appellant appealed to this Court by special leave. HELD: (1) The onus was heavy on him to prove its execution. [446C] (2) The propounder would be called upon to show by satisfactory evidence that the Will was signed by the testator, that the executant at the relevant time was in a sound and disposing state and of mind and that it represented her intentions. The onus is heavy on the appellant to establish by satisfactory proof that the testatrix fully understood the nature and effect of dispositions before she put her signatures to the will. [546C D] (3) The evidence of the appellant on the question of execution of the will has to be considered. If it had found in favour or against the appellant, the onus was burden on him. In this case no doubt the Calcutta High Court has held that it was not shown that the propounder did not at all support the appellant because his case must inevitably fail when it is held that he did not know the contents of the document before he put her initials to the Will. [646C E] (4) The High court was in error in coming to the conclusion that it had been proved to have known the provisions of the instrument before she placed her signature to the testator.

The appellant company was a dealer in Arc Carbons, manufactured by the appellant company. The appellant company had its factory at Hyderabad and it had its own factory at Bombay. The respondent company had purchased certain goods from the appellant for use as parts of motor vehicles. The goods were sold to agriculturists for agricultural purposes. The Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal held that they fall within entry 41 of Schedule 1 of the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1957, (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act '). The High Court also held that the use of the term "accessories" in item No. 4 of Schedule I of the Act was not an essential part of a type writer so as to attract the tax under entry 18 of the second schedule to the Mysore Sales Tax, Act, 1958 (hereinafter called 'the [Act '). In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the sales tax authorities were wrong in holding that they fell within entry 40 of Schedule II of the Andhra Pradesh General Sales tax Act, 1956. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The word "accessory" is used in the schedule to describe goods which may have been manufactured for use in projectors or other cinematographic equipment. It will be noticed that the expression "required for use" has been employed in several entries such as entry No. Of course, even where an entry relates to parts manufactured for using a particular kind of instrument of gadget only, the article would not cease to be covered by the intended entry merely because a purchaser makes some other use of it. [620G H] 2. The words "parts thereof" are used in several Entries such as Entry No. of course, though generally used in many entries, but excludes certain other articles by putting in the words "not being such articles as are ordinarily used for other purposes than as (1) (1965) 16 S.T.C. (2) (1970) 26 S. T.C.(3) ( 1970) 26S.T..C. The entry No, 4 occurs in a schedule in which descriptions of goods to be taxed indicate that the expressions "accessures" and include "other cinematographer equipment". But excludes certain others by putting into the words 'not being so used for use", such as entries Nos. Of Course, even though an entry relating to parts produced for use is made for equipment or accessories connected with the main purpose. [720G] 3. The expression "accessor" is not used in any of the entries but excludes some other articles which are required for use. It would be noticed from the fact that they are known as "cinema arc carbons". But excluding certain other items by putting In the words used in various entries such like entry No., Of course even where a purchaser make some other uses of it, could not detract from the classification to which the carbon arcs belong. [820F] 4. The fact that the goods under consideration are covered by an entry meant for use only as "accessaries" would not be a decisive factor in determining whether the goods fall within the relevant entry or not. [820G H; 821A B] 5. The entries Nos, Of Course and Practice, even if they are not known in the commercial world as "electrical goods", could not be regarded as parts. [824D F] 6. The term " accessories" is employed in various Entries such that the word "require for use has been used for equipment and accessories connected therewith. It cannot be satisfactorily determined in the light of the language of the entry itself considered in the context in which it occurs. [828A B C] 7.

The petitioners in these petitions challenged the validity of a notification issued by the Government of Gujarat on June 26, 1985 amending the Gujarat Minor Mineral Rules 1966. The petitioners contended that the royalty levied and covered under the rules should be applied only for mineral development and could not be used for any other purpose. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1.1 The impugned notification in question was in contravention of clause (b) of Article 304 of the Constitution. [419D] 1.2 The Act is passed for devel opment of minerals, but while discharging its functions relating to development, if the State incidentally allows mining to be carried on in the public interest and levies in that connection a tax, it does not mean that the said tax should be used only for development of minerals and not for other purposes sanctioned by law. [416E] 1:3 The Act was passed for decal opment and development of minor minerals, and for purposes connected there with. Rule 18 of the Rules provides for the determination of the rate of royalty payable in respect of minor mineral. The original rule 21 was substituted by new rule 21 by the issue of impugned notification on 26 6 1985 which provided that a holder of a Parwana granted under the Rules shall pay royalty at the rate prescribed for the time being in the rules framed by the State Government in respect o minor minerals except in the case of specified minor mineral and 20 hec tares in the cases of ordinary sand, Kankar Murram Gravel and in the ease of ordinary Sand, Kikar Murram and gravel a lease can be granted upto three years, and the area or land covered by a mining lease is governed by rule 15 which says that no quarry lease shall be granted for an area exceeding 10 hectares in case of any specified minor minerals. So a comparison of the relevant rules would show that a larger restriction was imposed both on the area in respect to which a Parna could be issued and the duration of the Parwana right and as also stated that the persons who take quarrying Parwana are persons belonging to the weaker sections of society and if under rule 21 a concession is shown in their favour it cannot be said that there is no reasonable nexus between the classification for purposes of the proviso to rule 21 to show concession in the matter of payment of royalty and the social policy underlying the Constitution, the statute and the Rules. [414G H; 414A B] 1 :4 The fact that section 15 of the Act does not authorise the State Govern ment to show such concession while promulgating the Rules which are in the nature of subordi nate legislation is also of no consequence. No express power need to conferred on such subordinate authority in order to make a classification for purpose of implementing the policy of the statute under which the Rules are made. [413C D] 1.:5 The fact, that section 17 of the Gujarat Mineral Rules, 1966 does not authorize the State Govt. to show any such concession when promulgating rules which are inconsistent with the provisions of Article 301 of the Constitu tion regarding movement of goods from one State to another for the activity of quarrying do not involve any movement as such. [ 413D] 2.1 In order to achieve this object, the Legislature has enacted the Gujarat minor Mineral Rules 1967. Rule 21 of the rules provides that a person who takes mining lease or any other mineral conces sion granted under any rule made under sub section (1) shall pay royalties at the rates specified in column 1 of the schedule, removed or consumed by him or by his agent, manager, employee, contractor or sub lessee from the leased area at the Rate prescribed for that purpose. Rule 19 provides for determination of royalty in respect Of minor minerals and for matters connected therewith.

The appellant was a hereditary trustee of the temple. He took a different view and proceeded on the basis that trusteeship of the Kumaran Koil was not hereditary. The Subordinate Judge held that the appellant was not a hereditary tenant within the meaning of section 6(9) of Madras Act 19 of 1951. On appeal by the respondents, the High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment of the Subordinate Judge Nagapattinam. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the succession was "regulated by usage" and that according to the usage of the Temple the trustees were elected for a period of one year each at a meeting of the members of the Sangunatha Mudaliar Community and so the appellant must be held to be a trustee within the ambit of section 4(9). HELD: (i) The word "succession" in section 6 (9) is identical in both the Acts. [446 B] (ii) It is not possible to say that there is a succession of As office to another when on the efflux of the period for which A was appointed, there is an vacancy and B is elected to that vacancy. [427 C D] (iii) The definition of hereditary trustee in section 2(9)(a) of the Act would include even such cases. But the election to the office of trustee in the present case is for a fixed period of two years and not for life. It is, therefore, difficult to hold that there was a succession within As office. [544 E F] (iv) The appellant 's contention that the trusteeship was "occupied by hereditary right or because succession to that office is by nomination by the holder in office" is not correct.

The appellant was a member of the Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly. He was arrested on April 26, 1971 at about 10.00 P.M. The prosecution case against him was that he had been sleeping on a bench outside his cattle shed in the open space, which is shown in the site plan (exhibit P15) at No. The younger brother of the deceased, Pandurangam, who was also sleeping on the eastern parapet of the sluice of the north Boothagudi channel, was also sitting on the western side of the Sluice. He had gone to his house and saw PWs 1, 2 and 3 chasing Karunakaran while running away after the assault was over. The accused was arrested at about 11.00 A.M., and he was shown as an absconder. On April 26 the evidence of PW 4 was recorded by the Magistrate under section 164 Cr. P.C. against the appellant. The High Court held that "PW 4 who was afflicted with the fell disease of leprosy, has completely given a go by to this statement and stated in the first information report that the deceased chased him from behind. It is also possible that those persons who gathered would not ask PW 4, who arrived at the place a little later, for information with regard to the assailants. The fact that the witness had stated in his first information Report that the appellant was only mentioning the name of accused Karunakaran as his assailant, this earlier version appears to be contradicted by the testimony in court on a very material point." On appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the High Court "can place no reliance on the testimony of PW 1, (2) the evidence given by him is not reliable; (3) the eye witness could be persuaded to substitute PWs 1 and 2 for his deceased brother as chasing the assailants, degrades them from the status of an absolutely reliable witness. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High court was not right that PW 4 stands wholly corroborated by the contents of the FIR. [723C] (4) The very fact that this eye witness had deposed in the second information report is true that the accused was also running away from the place where he fell dead. It also stands to reason that those person who gathered after the incident a little earlier than PW 4 did not see the assailants who might have already escaped. [823C D] (5) The High 'Court was not justified in convicting the appellant on the sole testimony of this solitary eye witness.

The respondents were the heirs and legal representatives of Amarchand who died in the previous year. The Income tax Officer assessed the total income of the deceased Amarchand to income tax under section 24B(1) read with section 24A of the Income tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that on a correct interpretation of section 24 B the amounts which were received by the heirs or legal representatives after his death should be deemed by the fiction incorporated in sub section (1) to be income received by Amarchand and liable to tax under s.24B(2). On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal held that the income was taxable as the estate was liable for tax on the amounts received by her husband and that the Income Tax Officer was entitled to assess the total Income of the said deceased Amar Chand. The High Court in reference held that section 24BB did not apply to the case of the respondents and that section 23B was applicable only to cases where the income had already been received before his death but not after his lifetime. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The fiction is limited to the cases provided in the three sub sections of section 1, 2 and 3 of s. 24B. [707 G] (ii) The legal representatives have by fiction become liable for payment of income tax out of their estate. They are not liable to be taxed as income received after his demise but they are liable to pay out of the estate of the person who cannot be deemed to be assessees for the purpose of assessment in the several years of assessment. [807 C] (iii) The Explanation to section 24(1)(b) does not apply where a person dies before the publication of the notice referred to in sub s.(1) of section 22 or before he is served with a notice under sub section(2) of that section. It cannot be extended beyond the object for which it was enacted. [777 D] (iv) The words "any tax which would have been payable by him under this Act if he had not died" indicate that they were income which may be deemed as taxable by fiction incorporated into sub s. (1). In the present case the amounts claimed to be taxable were those which were not received in the earlier year and were therefore not liable for taxation in the subsequent years.

The petitioners who were members of the Andhra Pradesh State Public Employment (Requirement to Residence) Rules, 1959 challenged the validity of the impugned orders on the ground that they contravened article 16(3) and Article 16(1) of the Constitution. The High Court quashed the orders holding that the power was given to Parliament under article 35(a) of tile Constitution and that the petitioners were not entitled to any relief under article 32 of the constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that (i) the power to make a law prescribing requirement as to residence in a part of a State is not conferred by Parliament, and (ii) the Rules are ultra vires the Constitution and were therefore void. HELD: The contention that the impugned order is invalid cannot be accepted. It was not necessary for the Legislature to specifically provide for residence in any particular part of the State or any particular Part of it. [122 G] (i)(a) The power to legislate is given to the Parliament but is denied to the Legislatures of the States, notwithstanding anything in the Constitution, and under that Article the Parliament has been supreme and can make any law on the subject as the article stood, speaks of a whole State as the venue for residential qualification and it is impossible to think that the Constituent Assembly was thinking of residence in Districts, Taluqas, cities etc. more appropriate and specific language could have been used as such or any requirement as aforesaid could have be used as some 'any requirement as mentioned in article 35 (a) and (b). [122 C D] (ii)(a)(i) The expression "any requirement" is not defined in the Act but it has been defined in section 3 of the Act. It means a condition of employment in the State, or Union territory prior to such appointment or employment. [123 G H] (b) The word 'any ' in article 16 (3) refers to residence within that State and includes any requirement which is necessary for residence within the State. The expression 'any other requirement as contemplated by article 35 has been used in the context of residence within a State or Union Territory prior to appointment or appointment to an office under the Government of, or any local authority within its territory. [124 A B] (c) The words "any requirements" in article 15(3), are wide enough to include residence within one State and not necessarily within that other State. [125 C D E] (d) The object of the Article is to provide for a special case for the establishment of residence outside the State and for employment or appointment in any office under another State. It is not necessary that there should be a separate provision for residence of persons belonging to different States. [126 A B, 127 C D]. (e) The first clause emphasises that the requirement may be also as to residential qualification but it is difficult to think whether Parliament 's intention in this behalf was to make any such law on a subject as a condition or employment in that State or part of that State. If it chose to speak of residence, in parts of State, as it stood, there would be no question of delegation to the Central and/or State Governments to provide by rules for the further implementing of the law made by Parliament.

The appellant was a postman attached to the Bulandshahr post office. He was tried for offences under section 52 of the Indian Post Office Act, 1898 and in two of ' them he was convicted for an offence under sections 467 and 471 of the Penal Code. The Additional Sessions judge acquitted him on appeal by the State. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the prosecution having merely shown that the registered letters were recovered from an almirah in the house in which the appellant lives jointly with his father, the presumption could be drawn against him that he had secreted them from the mere fact that they were found in the almirah which was said to have been in his exclusive possession; (2) that the almirah contained a large number of articles belonging to the father and since he had the opportunity to get at the articles lost all significance and can possibly have no bearing on the question as to the nature of possession attributable to the appellant. HELD: The prosecution having failed to prove that these letters were in the exclusive possession of the appellant, this presumption could not be drawn under section 53 of the Act; (3) that even if the locked almirah contained some articles belonging either to the mother and father, it would not be legitimate to infer that he was in possession of those articles and then infer that the lwpukable article was not in his own exclusive possession. [419D] The prosecution has been able to prove its case beyond all reasonable doubt. It is sufficient to point out that though the locked receptacle contained a small number of items belonging to him, certain other articles belonging thereto were in his possession. If the point to be 418 established was whether the almirah containing the key with him was even in the appellant 's exclusive possession along with his mother because he had an opportunity to procure them from postal articles kept or lying in the post office, the legislature has deliberately enlarged the scope of section 52 so as to include secretion, destruction or throwing away of postal articles by an officer of the post Office even though they may not have been entrusted to him or even though the are riot articles with which he is required or is competent to deal in the course of his duties.

The appellants were convicted of contempt of court and sentenced to pay a fine of Rs. 1,000/ and further ordered that in case of default they shall undergo simple imprisonment for two weeks. The High Court held that the Nyaya Panchayat had no jurisdiction to pass an order staying proceedings pending before the Nyaya panchayat. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court erred in holding that the Magistrate had no authority to decide the question whether the Nyaya Panchayats exercised judicial powers and, even if the Panch failed to do so, he could not be said to have committed contempt of Court. HELD : (i) The order sheet dated December 25, 1963 was an affidavit filed by the Sarpanch before a person authorised to administer oaths is not bound to do it and, therefore, the Nyaya panchayats exercised judicial power and even if they failed to comply with the directions given by the High court, they could not have proceeded further. [119 D E] (ii) The High Courts did not appreciate that the so called affidavit which was filed before the Panchas was in fact an affidavit at all. It had not been sworn to before any person authorised under section 12 of the Act can be said that he has committed contempt. [120 G H] (iii) The Magistrate had not taken cognizance of the application and the affidavit of Mahabir was not a certified copy of the order. [121 C D] (iv) The provisions of section 12(1)(a) of the , are mandatory in character, and they cannot be ignored merely because the Sarpanch had admitted in his deposition that he had to authority to tell Mahabir that his affidavit was not proper.

The appellant was convicted by the Sessions Judge under section 302, I.P.C., for causing the death of Sheo Sahai and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court dismissed his appeal against conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the entire report dictated by the appellant at the Police Station was inadmissible in evidence as its contents were not supported by any medical evidence, and that the extra judicial confession together with the circumstances relied on by the High Court had been wrongly rejected by the trial court. HELD : (i) The High Courts erred in rejecting the statement of the appellant about the appellant 's confessing to him that he had murdered Sheo Sahai. [211 G] (ii) The evidence of the approver was corroborated by Paley Singh, P.W. 2 who stated that the appellant had a bath in the Canal at night in the canal and had said that he did not see the appellant in the field on account of the crops being not very high. The fact that he was the sword which was stained with human blood at the time of murder is sufficient to establish conclusively that the person who possessed it so shortly after the murder of a person with whom he had enmity, had committed the murder. [212 B C] (iii) The extra judicial confessions of the accused to the police officer were not admissible in evidence under section 32 of the Evidence Act as there was good independent evidence with respect to the four matters mentioned in the report and relied on. [213 E] (iv) The statement made by the approver at the police station was inadmissible under section 8 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872. The statement of a co accused person recorded by the Magistrate was admissible under section 33 of the Act.

The appellants were elected as members of the Madhya Pradesh Munici 493 pal Corporation (Preparation, Revision and Publication of Electoral Rolls) Rules 1963. The election was challenged by some of the petitioners on various grounds including that the entire election process had become vitiated on account of the defect in the notice issued under Rule 4(1) of the Rules notifying that claims and objections should be preferred within a period of 20 days from the date of publication of the said notice before Shri K. S. Sharma, Deputy Collector without following the procedure prescribed for the purpose. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the election process was vitiated on the ground of non compliance with Rule 4 (3) of Madhya Pradesh Pradesh M�unici 49 pal Corporation Act, 1951 and that the declaration of results of all the 44 successful candidates was liable to be quashed. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellants that the petitioners were entitled to issue of the writ prayed for as of right and the delay in filing the petition should have been ignored. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The writ petition itself was presented on December 28, 1978. No satisfactory explanation was given in the course of the petition by the petitioners as to why they delayed the filing of the Petition till December 28. 1978 even though they knew that there was an error in the notices issued under rule 4(2) of Rules notifying the election and also called upon interested persons to prefer claims or objections thereto within a stipulated period. [417C D] 2. The Deputy Collector had asked petitioner No. 1 to file his claim and/or objection within a specified period. It was notified that the nominations could be filed on and after November 25, 1978 and the poll, if necessary, would take place on December 31, 1978, in all the 43 constituencies: Six petitioners including the appellants herein presented a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court of Madhya Pradesh Kumar Mishra vs State of M.P., [1978] 2 S.C.R. 829 and 16/79. The final publication of these electoral roll under Rule 8 was done on November 25. 1978. Thereafter the calendar of events was published on November 28, 1979 notifying that the poll if necessary would take places on December 30, 1978 in all 44 constituencies: six petitioners including petitioner No., They further pleaded that the authorities would have taken action to correct the error in notice issued Under Rule 4 of the rules prescribing that claims or objection should be made within a prescribed period. The petitioners were not entitled to the issue of such writ prayed as of rights and the delays in filing their petition should be ignored. [409D E] 3. The contention that the Collector had been informed about the defect was rightly rejected by the High court as there was no satisfactory explanation for the delay. [413E F] 4. The question whether the petitioners are entitled to a relief of right or the delay is one of fact and not of law. It is difficult to place any reliance on the said news item for the purposes of concluding that the District Magistrate had been intimated about the defects in the Notice issued under Rules 4(3) and (1). [413C D; 413A] 5. The Collector, Raipur had been apprised about the fact that there were an error apparent on the face of the record. He had asked petitioners No. 2 to file their claims and/ or objections within a particular period. No satisfactorily explanation was furnished in the petition as to how they delayed filing of petitions till December 31.

The company and its directors were prosecuted for failure to Me with the Registrar of Companies on or before 30 10 1967. The trial court acquitted the accused holding that the company and their directors could not rely upon their failure to call the general meeting as a defence to the prosecution. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decision of the trial court and convicted the accused under section 134(4) of the . The High Court held that the failure to send a copy of the balance sheet and profit and loss account before it could expose the person responsible to punishment under other provisions of the Act, it was obvious that no copies of such documents so laid should be filed before the Registrar. In appeal to this Court by special leave, it is contended on behalf of the appellant that the decision necessarily led to the conclusion that even in a prosecution under section 132(1) of .the 1913 Act (corresponding to section 220 of the 1956 Act) the company could not be heard to say in defence to a charge and so, if he was responsible for not calling the general meetings before it may expose the persons responsible to punishments under other sections of the , the balancesheet and profit loss before it might expose the petitioner to punishment udder section 220. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The decision necessarily lead to the inference that even though in a case under section 133(1)(3) of ,the obligation to file the list is independent of the holding of a general meeting, there can be no question of that balance sheet not being adopted nor of complying with the requirements of section 220 and hence, the persons concerned would be liable for punishment under sections 134(2) of The Companies Act or sub section (1) thereof. [435C D] 2. If no general body meeting is held, it can only be said that no copy of such document laid before a general body may have been forwarded under sub section(1). But if no general Body meeting is conducted, it cannot be said to be a condition precedent to the requirement that copies of the Balance sheet or profit and losses account before an annual general meeting are filed with the registrar. [427F] 3. The fact that section 26 makes the offence a continuing one also shows that the obligation to send copy of balance sheet or the profit and Loss account before the company may expose him to punishment Udder sections 134, 220 and 221 of the Old Companies Act and Section 220 of .hence it is made obligatory. But under section 135(1), the obligation should be for default in filing copies of a balance sheet, or the profits and loss accounts which are laid before the general body. [335F] 4. The failure to comply with the requirement of sub section 2 of section 134 of the New Companies Act is for default. But section 134 lays down that after balance sheet is laid before an ordinary general body, there shall be no objection to that balancesheet or profit or loss account being laid before it. [332A] 5. The provisions of both the Acts are clear and unambiguous. It is well settled that a person charged with an offence cannot rely on his default as an answer to the charge and he can be heard in defence only if he is responsible for non calling the company at such meeting. [333B] 6. In this case, the failure of the company to call a general Body Meeting and to lay the balance sheets and profit before it can expose the company responsible to penalty under other provision of the Companies Act, 1913 or section 220 Of the , cannot be held to make him liable udnder section 134 (4)of the Old companies Act or section220 of the ; [333C D; 334A] 7.

The appellant was convicted under section 5(1) of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1950, and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months. The High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to one year 's rigorous imprisonment. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the object of the impugned Act is to show that it is based on a reasonable classification of persons to whom or the offences in respect of which the procedure laid down in it is to apply and hence it is necessary to ascertain whether it is actually based on such a classification. The object of section 5 (1) is to provide for speedier trial of certain offences and not to punish any particular case or classes of cases or classes thereof, or class of cases as the State Government may by general or special order in writing direct. The Act does not contemplate a single trial of several offences but only one trial of all such offences. It is the State which has to make an application under section 6 (1), and it is the state government which can make the necessary classification for the purpose of making the provisions applicable to the procedure prescribed by it. The scheme of the Act shows that it was intended to provide a speediers trial of some offences, but not all offences or classes or cases as a whole. It does not by its own force make the special procedure provided in the Act applicable to all persons and to all offences, except those mentioned in section 5. The provisions of the statute are designed to achieve the object which is intended to be achieved by the Act. The classification of offences or the cases, for, in the absence of any special circumstances, cannot be regarded as a reasonable basis for classification.

The appellant was appointed as a Specialist Grade II in the Maulana Azad Medical College and treated as an Associate Professor of Radiotherapy in Maulana Safdarjang Hospital. The appellant was also working as a Reader/Assistant Professor in the said speciality. On November 9, 1964, he was promoted to the post of Assistant Professor in Radiotherap in the Medical College. He was confirmed as such by the Ma ul Azad Medical college and treated at the Maur Azad Medical Colleges. In the year 1965, the appellant was declared a Specialist grade II in a teaching hospital attached to the Maul Azad Medical University. The respondent No. 1, who was working as an Assistant Professor of radiotherapy, filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging his promotion and contending that he had acquired the essential educational qualification and experience requisite for appointment to the said post. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant possessed the qualifications and experience required for appointment by direct recruitment as well as by the Selection Committee. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the status of Associate Professor in a Teaching hospital attached with the Ma Ul Azad MedicalCollege is akin to that of honorary Professor or Associate Professor who has been actually teaching the students of the Ma Swami Azad Medical Hospital and the mere designation of the Appellant as such does not give him a right to hold the post. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The status of Assistant Professors of Radiology (ex officio) with effect from October 9, 1963 cannot be taken into consideration. [815E] 2.2 The designation of an appellant as Associate Professor is a clinical post while that of Associate professor in the Hospital attached to a Specialists Grade II like the appellant who, while holding a non- clinical post in a research institution attached to it, has been continuously teaching the courses of studies for the last 17 years. [915F] 3. The designation and status of the appellants as Associate Professors of radiography is a teaching post. That being so, it is urged that there is no distinction between the two posts of Radiologist and Associate Professor as the post in which of honorary professor or Associate Professors in the Willingdon Hospital or the Safdarjung hospital has beenMAN teaching the appellant as Radiologist cum Associate Professor. [1015G] 4. The status, status of superannuation of the respondent No 1 as a Professor of Pathology is a Teaching post and not an Associate professor. [1116C] 5.1 In view of the fact that the designation of a person as such is akin, it cannot be said that the respondent no. 1 has acquired the status as anAssistant Professor of pathology in Maur Patel Medical College to which it is affiliated. The mere designation and designation of his appellant as such do not give any right to holding the post as Associate professor of Radiologicalrapy in the Dr. Ambedkar Hospital or Safdarjhang Hospital, cannot be considered a right for appointment as Professor of Surotherapy. [1215D] 5:2 In view thereof, it would otherwise work great injustice to persons in Specialists grade II like that of Honorary Professor or Assistant Professors in Maul Patel Medical college to which they, while functioning as such, have been actually Teaching the students in the Post of Radiographer cum Associate Professors and Assistant Professors respectively. [1315E; 1316A] 5(a) The status and status Of Associate Professor and Assistant Professor is akin: that of receivable by the appellant from the Ma Dr. Nehru Medical College, New Delhi, and the Mere designation of such person does not giving him a Right to hold post of Associate Professors or Assistant Professor, cannot prevail.

The workmen of Orient Paper Mills Ltd., Brajrajnagar, have come up in this appeal by special leave against an award of the Industrial Tribunal, Orissa. The first and the main point argued was that the Tribunal had committed an error of law in fixing minimum wages in the Company on the basis of the average minimum wage prevailing in other industries in that region which could be compared with the Company 's case. Held, that the principle laid down by this Court in French Motor Car Co., Ltd. vs The Industrial Tribunal was not rigid and it is not necessary that the minimum wage should be fixed at the average level of 'wages in the other comparable industries in the region. In the instant case, however, there was nothing to show that the Company was providing any such amenities which were different from the amenities provided by those concerns in the regions which are being.compared with the company for the purpose of fixation of minimum wage Consequently, it would be more appropriate to compare the total wage packet of the Company with the wage packet received by the workmen of other industries In the case of even the lowest paid clerical staff, to whom dearness allowance is separately payable, the bonus is only calculated on the assumption that their wage is a consolidated wage consisting of the two 678 elements of basic wage and dearness allowance lumped together. The principle which is being applied is the simple one of calculating the bonus payable at the rate of three months ' basic wages in each case and in no case is the dearness allowance taken into account.

The assessee was carrying on construction contracts under the Railways as well as the Government. The Income tax Officer found that the assessee had failed to comply with the requirements of section 151(2) of the Act and therefore, he issued a notice under section 148 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1961. The assessee filed an appeal before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner against the order of the Income tax officer but the Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal on the ground that it did not comply with section 151 (2) and that the notice was invalid inasmuch as it did neither comply with nor comply with any requirements of clause (a) or (b) of section 147. The Revenue appealed to this Court by special leave. Held, that the Commissioner was satisfied that the Income Tax Officer had complied with the requirement of section 148 and section 151 of the , he just noted the word "yes" and affixed his signatures thereon. The report submitted by him under section 151 is not a mere reproduction of the words "whether on his own total income or, on the total income of any other person during the previous year". Held, further, that if only he had read the report carefully, he could never have formed an opinion that it was a fit case for the issue of a notice unders. 148. The word "Yes" in section 147 is not used in the sense of the term "yies" but it is used in its context in which it occurs. It is only when the requirements are satisfied, the Incometax Officer has no jurisdiction to issue a notice u/s 148. [810 E] The Commissioner was not satisfied that by reason of omission or failure on the part of these assessee to make a return under section 139 for any assessment year to the Income ' tax Officer or to disclose fully and truly all material facts necessary for his assessment for that year, income chargeable to tax has escaped assessment for the accounting year in question. The order sheet recording the reasons of the Commissioner is not an integral part of the record. It was merely a reproduction of section 152(2). The report of the Incometax Officer as required by section 151 does not mention any reason for coming to the conclusion that it is a fit one for the issuance of a notification under section 147, but it mentions only "the Income tax Officers" and affixing his signatures thereunder.

The appellant was a partner in a firm carrying on business of Sait Nagjee Purushotham and Co., Bankers, Piece goods and Yarn Merts, SaitNagjee Purushotsham and Company. The Income tax Officer assessed the appellant to income tax for the years 1948 49 and 1949 50. In appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner, the appellant contended that as a result of splitting up there was discontinuance of the original business at the date of partition and on such discontinuance the family became entitled to relief under section 25(3) of the Income tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Tribunal held that as the business was taxed under the Act of 1918, the assessee was not entitled to the benefits of section 25 (4) of that Act. On appeal by the appellant, HELD: (1) The appellate firm was entitled to benefit under section 26(2) before it can be said that there was a discontinuance of its original business and on which tax was charged under the Income Tax Act, 1918. [916D] (2) The mere fact that he was not taken on in the original assessment year also shows that the original partnership business was assessed under the provisions of the Indian Income tax law, 1922, and it is the business which had paid tax under the 1918 Act while the emphasis in sub section (4), is on succession to a person who, on April J., 1939, was carried on by another person. [1016B] (3) The very fact that the appellant was not taking on the original firm also shows the fact that there were two independent firms, for the document of October 30, 1943, shows that there is a family partition and some vilasams were allotted to the father and the rest to the son. [ 1016C] (4)(a) The business must have been charged to tax under section 27(2).

The appellant, a Hindu widow, filed a suit for partition of the properties in the Court of the Sub Judge, Khandappa. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the suit properties belonged to the joint family and that there was no prior partition and that the plaintiff was entitled to a 7/24th share. On appeal by the appellant, the High Court held that the property belonged to his joint family, that the decree of the trial court was not fully justified and that on a true view of law, the widow 's share must be ascertained by adding the share to which she is entitled at a notional partition during her husband 's life time and the share which she would get in her husband's life time. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that (i) the widow had no prior or partition; (ii) the suit property belonged only to the family, and (iii) the wife will take equally, each having one share in the coparcenary property on the hypothesis of a partition between himself and his sons. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The interest of a Hindu Mist coparcener shall be deemed to be the share in that property if a partition of that property had taken place immediately before his death. [724B] 2. In order to ascertain the share of the deceased in the property that would have been allotted to him if a division of the property had took place immediately prior to his death, there must be some evidence to show that the share was actually allotted to the appellant or she received or must be deemed not to have received in the notional partition. [765C] 3. The fictional, however, expedient to ascertain share of heirs in the ancestral property has to be determined according to the terms of the testamentary instrument if any, made by the deceased. In an important aspect, the case is stronger in the matter of working out the fictional that the interest of the Hindu Mist Mitakshara coparcener shall he deemed to have been given in the joint property because after all, the plaintiff 's husband and his children had a 1/4th share therein. [76B C] 4. The mere fact that there is no prior family partition or that there has been a partition during the life time between the plaintiff and his brothers does not make any difference. [77C D] 5. In the instant case, by application of the rules of intestate succession contained in sections 8, 9 and 10 of the Act, whatever be the shares of the coparcenary properties would devolve upon the surviving members of the family. The only step is to ascertain whether the share had actually taken place before his lifetime. [75E] 6. In a case where the plaintiff has a 1st share in a coparcenary property, the partition of which takes place immediately after his death is effected between him and his two sons, there would be four sharers in the family property on one side of a joint Hindu Family property. The first step also to ascertain what the share has actually taken from the deceased has to find out the share that the deceased had in the coparcener 's property. [78F G] 7. In view of this position, whatever was the share at the time of his death in the Mitakshara coparcenary property would devolve on the surviving member of the joint Hindu family. [79C D; 77A] 8. The High Court rightly held that there had been a severance of the interest and the plaintiff had no right to claim partition. The fact that the widow was not given any share in her ancestral property does not alter the position of the appellant 's father. [80F G].

The appellants were employees of the Corporation. They were appointed directly to Class I and Class II on or after 1st September, 1956. The Corporation had fixed the age of retirement in its service book. The appellants were not paid salary for the period from January 1, 1965 to March 31, 1966. On a representation made by them, the Government of India issued an order dated June 30, 1967 directing that the employees who joined the service of the corporation on or before 1st October, 1956 shall retire on completion of 58 years of age and at any time thereafter on giving three months ' notice or salary in lieu thereof. The appellant No. 1 was appointed directly as a Class III employee by virtue of the settlement and the amendment of the regulations. The employees who were appointed to Class II and Class IV irrespective of the fact whether they were transferred employees or employees appointed after 1 st September,1956 were entitled to continue in service till 60 years of their age subject to the usual clause relating to premature retirement. The respondents filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the order dated July 30, 1966 passed by the Government. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellants had not been paid salary from January 31, 1965 onwards and that they were entitled for payment of salary for that period. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that clause (b) of section 49(2) of the Act was not in terms applicable to the transferred employees who became the employees of Class III and Class I or Class II, as the case may be. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High court erred in striking down regulation 19(2). [776F] 2.1 It is only in 1965 under the settlement that the age was raised to 60 years on their being promoted to a Class I post or Class III post. [778G] 3.1 In 1965 under section 11 of the , the age limit for retirement of employees who had joined the services of the Corpo ration belonging to Class III or Class IV would be 58 years. The appointing authority may at its discretion extend his service for one year at a time upto 60 years, but the competent authority may, if it is of the opinion that it is in the interest of theCorporation to do so, direct such employee to retire on attaining the age o superannuation or at any stage thereafter on give him three months' notice or wages in lieu of notice or pay in lieu thereto. [77G] 4.2 The High Curt erred in upholding the validity and sustainability of the impugned order dated January 31., 1966 passed under section 49 (2) by the State Government. [773A B] 5.1 Section 49(3) of The Act was enacted to provide for the benefit of employees belonging to class I or class II categories appointed to the service on or After 1st August, 1956 and in respect of whom the Corporation has fixed the ages of retirement as 58 years which corre sponds to the age Of superannuation in almost all the public sector establishments, the Central Government services and the State Governments services. [777A B C] 5 2.3 The High Courts erred in holding that clause(b) was not applicable to those transferred employees whose appointment had joined service after 1St September, 1966 by virtue o the settlement. [779D F] 4 3.4 In 1965 the age fixed for retirement in Class III was raised from 60 years to 58 years only because he had been promoted to Class IV only till he attained the ageof 60 years as a class III employee. The provisions of section 11 were not applicable in the transferred employee who joined service before 1 st August, 1966 and who joined services after 1th September, 1957 by virtue Of the settlement dated June 19, 1965.

The appellants wrote a letter to the President of India, the Chief Minister of Haryana and the Chief Justice of Punjab High Court. The Chief Justice sent a letter on 20 February 1975 to the Prime Minister, Chief Minister, Haryana and Haryana High Court for being handed over to him for his personal attention. The appellants did not take any action against them. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the constitutional validity of the Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the contempt proceedings were dropped. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the letters were addressed by the deponent to the Chief Secretary, Haryana, and the Prime Ministers had no jurisdiction to take action against the persons who would criticise the Judge 's speech. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The letter in question did not constitute contempt of court. It was a mere communication addressed by one member of the Bar Association to another member of that association. [243E] 2. The contents of the letter were unchallenged and we are of opinion that the High Curt proceeded on the basis that there was no intention whatsoever on his part to scandalise the Hon 'ble Judge or this Hon ' ble Court or to lower the authority or undermine the prestige of the learned Judge or of the Hon'ble Court. [244E] 3. The letters in question were addressed to the District Bar Association, Bhiwani and were addressed at Charkhi Dadri. It is an article of faith with the deponent himself. Therefore, the deponent tender his apology to this Hon' ble Court for the same and prays for its acceptance. The deponent most respectfully submits that there is to be a finding of committal of contempt. [245G] 4. If in view of this Honble Court, the action of the deponent in addressing the letter in questions constituted for any reason contempt of Court, one would be more sorry than the deponent itself. Therefore the deponent tendered his apology. The affidavit in question does not constitute a contempt. It cannot be said that there has been any intention whatsoever by the appellants to scandalize the Hon.'ble Court or that the Judges concerned did speak on the matters ascribed to him before the court would take any step against the person who would criticize the Judge. [246E] 5. The contempt proceedings are dropped.

The petitioner was a registered dealer under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Income Tax Officer held that certain sections of the Taxation on Income (Investigation Commission) Act, 1947, were void from the date of commencement of the Constitution by reason of article 14 of the constitution and that the provisions of section 5(1) of the said Act were unconstitutional. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of sub section (4) of section 6 of the Act on the ground that certain provisions of the Indian Incometax Act, had become void from its date of the commencement of Constitution by virtue of article 19(1)(f) and that it was not competent to the Commission to make a report to the Central Government. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that sub section(4) did not confer any larger power on the Commission under the provisions Of the Indian income tax Act and that in any case the procedure prescribed by the Indian law was a good substitute for that prescribed by section 34 of the Income tax (Investigating Commission)Act, 1947. The appellant contended that the impugned Act violated article 14 inasmuch as it did not provide for an enquiry into the validity or otherwise of sub sections (1), (2), (3), (7) and (8) of Section 5 of the impugned act and that therefore the provisions contained in section 5 were void. Held, that the procedure to be followed by the Commission was a valid one and that there was no substantial difference between the two procedures. The procedure prescribed under section 34 was a fair substitute for the procedure laid down in section 7 which provides that subject to the provisions o sub section 4 of section 8 the Commission shall have power to regulate its own procedure and that procedure prescribed in section 34 is a good substituting for that provided by the Act. The provisions of sub clauses (3) of article 20 were not intended to be exhaustive or exhaustive but they were intended to operate only to the detriment of those dealt with under sub section 2(1). The procedure laid in section 8 was a complete code and did not offend any provision of law. The purpose of enacting sub section 3 of section 34 had been to ensure that the Commission could make an enquiry to ascertain whether there was substantial difference in the procedure for conducting investigation into escaped income or evaded income. The object of the legislation was to prevent evasion of tax on income both under section 5 and the procedure which prescribed by it. It was not intended that the provision contained in sub section should be so construed as to make it a part of the statute itself. The language used in section 4(4)(a) of Act, therefore, clearly showed that there could be no difference between those dealt under sub sections 2 and 3. The words "any person other than the person whose case or points in whose case is being investigated to rebut any evidence brought on the record against him" were intended only to cover cases where the investigation into an escaped income was limited to a maximum period of eight years, while under the Act it was open to the Government to make such enquiry as may be specified in that behalf. The section does not say that there is in this matter in the first stages some similarity in the procedures prescribed by sub sections 1, (2) and 3 which would operate to the prejudice of those persons dealt with thereunder. It only provides that for the purpose of enabling the person who whose case was or are being investigated, he shall on application made in this behalf and on payment of such fees as may been prescribed by rules, be furnished with certified copies of documents, statements, papers and materials brought on record by the commission.

The appellant, a "commercial establishment" carried on in the premises in question. The Federation was registered under the Delhi Shops and Establishments Act, 1954. It was carrying on business of manufacturing and selling goods. In the course of its activities, the Federation had been carrying on various kinds of trade and commerce. The Association was formed for the purpose of carrying on certain types of trade or business in connection with, or incidental to, the objects of the Federation. The appellant was a "Commercial Establishment" within the meaning of section 2(5) of the Act which, in consequence had no application. "The Federation failed to comply with the direction and contended that it was not an "establishment" as defined in section 2 (9) of that Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the activities carried on by the Federation were a business or trade. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1 The definition of "commercial Establishment" in section2(j) of is far wider than that of " commercial establishment". [352A B] 2.1 It is immaterial whether its activities bring its premises within the ambit of a "shop" or a " commercial Establishment" because by the Memorandum of Association, Articles of Association and other material, which was more or less the same as in the present case, it was held that these activities of the appellant were also in the nature of material services within the wider definition of 'commercial establishment". The fact of the matter is that the Federation also publishes periodicals, bulletins etc. and issues the same to member free of this Court in R. K. Of course, that profit is ploughed back for the purposes of the Union as set out in its Memorandum of association, and is not distributed among its members. [352C D] 2:2 The mere word "trade" does not necessarily mean something by which a profit is made. It will bear repetition that the definition of the word "business" in s.2(h) of Act is far narrower than that in section. 2(j). [352B C] 3:3 In the instant case, before the High Court, it had not argued that the activity of the Association was not a "trade", business or profession. The fact that the respondent is a Federation of Federations and not an association of any individual traders, industrialists or businessmen cannot, by any stretch of reasoning, be called a "business". [353C D; 353A] 4:4 In the very definition of a 'commercial Establishment", it indicates that the function of a registered society, charitable or other trust will not take it out of the definition if the activity carried on is a business. It would bear repetition to say that the mere word 'trade ' does not automatically mean something By which a profits is made, and it will bear added that the concept of mere word is used in the Act. [353F] 5:5 The fact whether the activities of a Federation are also in nature of materials services within its wider definition indicates that these activity of a society, Charitable or other Trust will not come within the definition unless the activity carries on business or commerce. It does not mean something which by itself amounts to a busi (1)[1971] 1 S.C.R. Mittal 's case, ; , referred to.

The assessee was a Hindu undivided family headed by one Sri Trivikram Narain Singh who was the original founder and owner of certain lands. The Income tax Officer held that it was a regular annual income of the assessee and did not fall within the category of agricultural income tax. He observed that "in fact this income arose from a statutory obligation of the Government to pay it, and though the Government recouped this from the person with whom the land was settled, land in the genealogical tree of Malikana appears in the second degree, its immediate and effective source is the Government 's statutory obligation to pay the same, and that is so, notwithstanding that computation of remuneration is made as a percentage of the income, a substantial part whereof is derived from lands used for agricultural purposes. " The Appellate Tribunal held that the right which was conferred by the letter dated July 7, 1837, no right in the land revenue was granted to the assessee. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the income of a trust appropriated by the Government for extinguishing proprietary rights of the Jagirdar and when the immediate source of the Income was not land or rent collections from land, it is difficult to hold that the receipt of the respondent was agricultural income within the meaning of section 4(3)(viii) of the Act. HELD: (i) The right conferred on a person by an instrument of trust is a right to receive and appropriate to himself the income or revenue of land, but rests in the covenant in the deed to receive remuneration for management of the trust. [739 E] (ii) The source of income is clearly the arrangement arrived at in 1837 and, therefore it is not agricultural income as defined in the Act; and (iii) the receipt was merely a measure, and indicated the source of this right in lieu of which the allowance was given. [758 D] (iii)(a) The income of an assessee is not taxable under the Indian Income tax Act. It is true that the income can be held to be derived from land within the ambit of the definition in section 2(1)(a). But in this case no material has been produced to show that the allowance varied from year to year, the source and character of the receipt are, therefore, altered when a part of the net income of trust was appropriated by him as his remuneration. [759 E F] (b) The amount of pension is not received by the assessee as rent or revenue. It follows from the decisions of the Privy Council and the judgments of this Court cited above that if it is held in this particular case that the source is clearly arrangement arrived into in 1838, then the income cannot be held income derived from the land within its meaning of the term in section 4 (3)(ix) of Income tax.
