[444B C] 1 :5.1 In view of t his matter to put them at par it would be appropriate that t the petitioners who had been recruited in 1963 and were appointed in subsequent yo rs could not be promoted inasmu ch as by the time their cases could be considered for promoti on the subsequent order dated 28th December, 1965 and had come in force. [445C D; 446A] 2.2 In view o f the matter to give them in the said Civ il Appeal the same benefits as were given by the Madhya Pradesh High Court to such of the petitioners before that Court w ho were Supervisors 'A.' and were granted promotion as Foreman Grade I on expiry Of 2 years from the date they were promoted. [443D E] 1 3.3 The circular dated 5th November 1962 and circular dated 21st January 1966 are completely silent on the point and the appeal w as allowed only on the ground that some Supervisors having been en promoted as chargemen II and certain others had not been promoted as Foreman I on ly due consideration of the circular dated 29 th December, 1963.

The Karnataka State Tourism Development Corporation, the appellant in these appeals, was granted permits for operating in any inter State route. The State Transport Undertaking applied for stage carriage permit from a State Transport undertaking for operating on the route. On the basis of the said application, the State Transport Authority granted permits to the private operators. The appellants filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the validity of the permits and also the validity thereof. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the proviso to section 63(7) did not offend article 14 of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the State transport Appellate Tribunal and the High court were wrong in distinguishing the decision of this Court in Sher Singh 's case and that the fourth sub clause of the proviso was unconstitutional and violative of article 14. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The word 'preference ' occurring in section 47(1 H) does not mean mere passing of an approved scheme or a notification by the State Government to the effect that it would be effective from the date on which the scheme is sanctioned. [1015C] 2. The proviso to sec. 63(1) does no say for example, like section 68 F(1), that the permit shall be granted to the State Undertaking. It only provides that in the case of inter State routes, the Undertaking will have preference in the matter of stage carriage permits. [ 1015C D] 3. The general scheme of the Act in the context of grant of permits for stage carriages and contract carriages appears to be that except in the cases of a notified route or notified area, where under section 68F(1)(a) the permit has to be necessarily granted to such State Transport Undertakings in all other cases, the claims of all eligible applicants must be considered on merits, applying the rules of preference wherever the claims are approximately equal. [1005D] 4. The words 'preferably grant ' occurring therein cannot mean mere making of an application for stage Carriage permit from one State to another. It is not necessary that the applicant should have a certificate of approval from the Central Government because of the rule of preference contained in proviso to Section 63(2). [1016E] 5. The expression 'preferential grant ' appearing in section 68D(1H) does mean only an application made for stage transport permit from another State Transport Corporation and not a mere application for a stage carriage Permit. It does not say, for example that like section68 F(I)(a), the permit had to be invariably granted to a State transport Undertaking. [102E] 6. The sub clause (iv) of the provisos to section63(7), is unconstitutional and it cannot be said that the application made by the applicant for stage stage carriage stage carriage was not for tourist vehicles or travel agents. [103F G] 7. The second proviso to s. 63 (7) is unconstitutional, and it is struck down as violative of Article 14 of Constitution. [104G H] 8. The third proviso to sub section (7), does not state that the permits shall be given preference overall other applications. It merely provides for preference to be given under section 47 (1H).

The respondent was a dealer in business of selling goods. The appellant, who was the registered owner of the business, sold the goods to the respondent on October 5, 1956 and the sale proceeds were credited into the account of the respondent. The respondent filed a suit for arrears of sales tax due from him on the ground that he had purchased the goods from the State Government as a dealer under section 19(1) of the Madras General Sales Tax Act 1939 (Madras Act IX of 1939). The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court in second appeal confirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that Rule 21 A is ultra vires of the rule making power of the State Govern ment under section19(1)(a) of Madras General sales Tax Act, 1939 (Mad. IX of 1940). HELD: The word 'assessment ' used in section 19 (2)(c) does not include the power of recovering tax assessed from a person other than the assessee. It follows therefore that Rule21 A is beyond the rule made by the State Legislature under section 9(1), and cannot be utilised to enlarge the scope of section 10 regarding recovery and payment of tax from some other person other persons other than a "dealer" under the Act. [665 B C] The word assessment ' has been defined in section 2(c) of that Act as including all proceedings taken under the Madras Sales Tax (3rd Amendment) Act, 1956. Therefore, Rule 21A is beyond its rule making powers of the state Government either under section 10 or section 19 of the Act and cannot he utilised to extend the scope thereof to any particular person other wise.

The appellant was a public servant. He was dismissed from service on the ground that it contravened article 311(2) of the Constitution. The State of Gujarat appealed to this Court by special leave. HELD : (i) The liability to pay arrears of salary earned by a public Servant for the period that he was actually in office is the liability of the State of Bombay and not of the Government servant for the time during which he has served. [922 D] (ii) The decree of the High Court decreeing payment of arrears of pay is truly a liability in proceedings relating to a contract within section 60(2)(a). It is true that some elements of relationship between a public officer and Government are based on contracts within the meaning of section 60 of the Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960. But so far as the State is concerned, some elements are of relationship inter se between a private servant and Government servants within the ambit of section 61. [ 922 E] (iii) The words ,actionable wrong other than breach of contract ' in this context are wide words and include something more than torts, but even so where a suit is brought by a Government servant against arrears of wages, the decree more properly falls under section 60. [961 D] In the instant case, the plaintiff was not concerned with the second contention but it was a dispute between the State and the State Government of Gujarat. The liability for payment of salary was not a liability arising out of a contract but was a liability which in fact arose wholly within the territory of the state of Maharashtra or the State.

The plaintiffs ' land lies immediately to the south of the defendants ' land. The plaintiffs alleged that the respondents had encroached upon their coal mines on the southern side and removed coal from the encroached portion and had rendered the remaining coal of the encroached portions unworkable. The appellants contended that the suit was not barred by limitation, because they were bound to keep a barrier of 25 feet to the north of the defendant 's working and, therefore, the boundary could more satisfactorily and definitely be fixed with reference to the plans annexed to the subsequent lease deeds executed in favour of the successors in interest of the appellant and the respondents. The trial court held that the defendants had knowledge of the sinking of the quarries and pits in the encroached land. Held, that the plaintiffs were bound by the tenor of the article in the Limitation Act and also to the rules of evidence. The High Court accepted the finding of fact arrived at by the courts below on the assumption that the initial burden was on the respondents to prove that they had knowledge about the existence of the said encroachment only within three years thereof. In other words, the onus of proof to establish knowledge on the part of the respondents beyond the prescribed time was on them to prove the possession of the converted property and that is all. The defendants did not deny the fact that the entire burden was upon the defendants. They did not admit the fact in their written statement that they came to know of the removal of coal by the appellant or their possession of their coal removed beyond three years of the date of filing of the suit. In the absence of any acceptable evidence on their part, the High Court could not have accepted the findings of the courts that the earlier burden was discharged by them within three months of the filing of their written statements.

The appellant was a crosscutter. The Secretary and others were charged with misconduct under r. 18(a) of the Standing Orders. The appellant challenged the validity of the order on the ground that it was not a bona fide exercise of the power conferred by r. 19(a). Held, that the Industrial Court had the right to inquire into the causes that might have led to termination of service even under a rule like 18(A) and if it is satisfied that the action taken under such a rule was a colourable exercise of power and was not bona fide or was a result of victimisation or unfair labour practice it would have jurisdiction to intervene and set aside such termination. The Industrial Court in its opinion had the power to inquire from the causes which might have lead to termination and if the terminaton of service is a colourable exercising of the powers conferred, it would be an colourable exercise Of the power under that rule. In the present case the tribunal held that the exercise of powers was colourable and it could not be said that view was incorrect. The Tribunal had the jurisdiction to inquire whether there was in fact misconduct and therefore the action was taken under r 18(b) by leading evidence before the tribunal to show that there was misconduct and, therefore, the action took under r, 18(c) was bona fide and was therefore not colourable exercise. The employer could defend the action under r., 18(d). Held further, that in a case of this kind the requirement of bona fides is essential and if an employee wants to take action for misconduct and then suddenly dropped the departmental proceedings which were intended to be held and decided to discharge the employee under r . 18(e) it is now well settled that even in a cases where the employer wanted to take disciplinary action against an employee instead of following the course of holding an inquiry for misconduct actually charged might be done away with. The industrial court cannot inquire into causes that may have led a result to termination.

The appellants were the tenants of a building in Ahmedabad. The respondent landlord filed a suit for declaration that it was entitled pursuant to the agreement dated December 1, 1960, to exhibit motion pictures in the theatre and for an injunction restraining the defendants from violating the said rights of Filmistan under the agreement. The Trial Court held that the consent decree had not decided that the transaction between the parties of the year 1954 was in the nature of a lease; that the suit No. 149 of 1960 was for declaration of the rights of the Filmistans to exhibit Motion pictures in theatre under the terms of the said agreement dated November 27, 1954 and for injunction restraining defendants from interfering with their possession. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that the question whether the legal relationship arising out of the agreement between December 1. 1960 was in existence or not was decided by the consent order of December 1., 1960; that in the plaint in the earlier suit it was not even averred that the rights granted were in the character of leasehold rights; that it related to a matter to be decided by a Court and on which the opinion of witnesses was irrelevant. The appellants contended that the agreement was not a lease ? HELD : (i) The question whether in fact the subordinate Court has decided the question of res judicata is one which is not vested in it by law. [419 C] (ii)The order passed by the High Court is set aside and the Trial Court is directed to proceed and dispose of the suit. [420 B] (iii)The question whether a legal relationship arose out of an agreement dated October 27, 1955 was already concluded by the Consent decree in suit No 149 of 1961. The only thing that can be said is that so far as the agreement of November 27. 1954 is con cerned, it must be held, in view of the consent judgment of December l., 1960, that that document created a lease. [ 420 E] (iv)The High Court has recorded a finding that the document dated November 28, 1954 created a tenancy and that the said consent decree operated as res judicata. The order passed in suit no 149 of 1958 had not been decided that it did not decide that question. It was for the Trial court to decide whether the transaction was in fact barred by res judicata or estoppel under the provisions of section 92 of the Evidence Act. [416 G H] (v)The Court has not recorded a findings on the question as to whether the document executed was a lease or of other character had to be determined at the trial and the previous judgment being a judgment by consent , 'could not operate as resjudicata, for it was only a finding of fact. [414 G] (vi)The agreement dated March 27,1954 created a leasehold interest in the cinema theatre under which the appellants were tenants. The document created lease was not one of the conditions precedent to the applicability of section 28 of the Bombay Rent Control Act. It did not create any tenancy or right in the building.

The respondent was appointed as a Pilot Officer in the Indian Air Force and was working as a pilot Officer. In the year 1972 he was declared unfit by a Medical Board and was, therefore, inval idated from I.A.F. The Government of India issued a scheme for the benefit of ex military officials. The State of Uttar Pradesh also adopted the same scheme. The term of the respondent had come to an end on 30th August, 1985 as stated above and no further order of extention had been passed by the Governor. In this connection it was contended that the interim order granted in favour of the respond ent was not in the nature of a contract and the subsequent orders extending his period of appointment till 30th of August,1985 were liable to be ignored and that he should be treated as a person regularly appointed in Government service entitled to con tinue till he completed the age of 58 years. The High Court allowed the Writ Petition holding that the termination order could not be sustained and the Writ petition was liable tobe dismissed. In appeal by special leave it was submitted on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had while setting aside the order of termination by its order dated 24th March, 1988 directed that the respondent was entitled to salary upto the period he was entitled for remain in service and further observed that it was open for the opposite parties to consider the claim of the petitioner for continu ation in service or of fresh appointment and no observations in this regard were made by the Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The respondent had not urged before the High court that the order dated 9th July, 1986 passed in his case was not an order of extension of service. If the respond ed was really aggrieved by the judgment dated 24.3.1988 he should have preferred an appeal before this Court and that was not right in making an order on Review on 26.7.1988 relying upon the interim orders dated 10th July 1986 passed by this Court during the pendency of the Writ Appeal. [243E F] 2. The interim order did not and could not amount to a direction that the respondents were entitled to be reinstated in service irrespective of the merits of the case and the extent of his right. [244F] 3. The order dated 10.7,.86 passed by High Court on review and restore the Judgment dated 24/3. 1988 passed in the Writ Petitions. The Interim order did neither and could have been amount to an direction that he was not entitled to remain in serv beyond 30th September, 1985 unless there was a further extension. [245G] 4. The writ petition was dismissed by this court on the ground of delay. [246F] 5. In view of the fact that no order of 'extension had been sanctioned by the Government beyond 30.8.1985, the respondent could not have filed an appeal against the judgment of the High Curt. The stay order did nothing but only a direction to the effect that the Respondent was entitled only to remain on service till he attained the age Of 58 years and further directed that he be treated in service even though there was no order from extension of services.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to suffer imprisonment for life. The prosecution case was that the deceased Subhadramma was the wife of the appellant and she used to stay in the house of the deceased 's mother. She was married about one and a half years before the occurrence. The accused used to visit his wife and often used to keep her in the same house. The deceased was also assaulted by the accused with a knife which he was carrying on his wife. The appellant was acquitted by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the discrepancies found by the Sessions Judge were of a minor character and that they have been unduly magnified by the learned Sessions Judge. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court should not interfere with the order of acquittal merely because another view is also possible. [368E] 2. In the instant case, the prosecution tried to make out a strong suspicion against the appellant that he was stabbing his wife in the manner suggested by the prosecution and when two views were possible, the benefit of doubt should be given to the accused. The evidence which is corroborated by the medical evidence on record shows that the injuries must have been caused in the way suggested by P.W. 1 to 3 or the evidence of P. W. I to 3. [367F G] 3. In view of the evidence which was corroborated by what was mentioned in exhibit P. 1, the appellant could not be said to have been prejudiced by the possibility of a duality of views, the High court should not interference with the orders merely because other view is possible. The appeal must accordingly fail. [369G H] 4. In order to entitle an accused person to the benefit Of doubt arising from the possibility Of a dual line of views the prosecution must be beset with fanciful doubts, rejects evidence for slender reasons and takes a view of that evidence in favour of the accused must be reasonable. [370B C] 5. The fact that some of the villagers who had gathered there were two divergent versions given by the Prosecution and the defence and when one views were available, the accused is entitled to the benefits of doubt. [371F G H] 6. In a case where an order of conviction is reversed, the appellate court should interfere with it only because another reasonable view is equally possible. If the evidence is so strong against the accused, the Court should interfere in the interest of justice lest the administration of justice be brought to ridicule.

The appellant was a Judge of the High Court. He was appointed as a Judge in the year 1952. On his appointment he was transferred to the High court. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Curt, contending that the sanction under Section 6 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 is not necessary for prosecution of a person holding such an office and that the same can be taken only if it is read as a part of the scheme under which the public servant is required to furnish particulars of his assets with reference to which the disproportion and his inability to satisfactorily account can be inferred. The High Court dismissed the writ petition, but on appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The power to punish a Judge or Chief Justice of India is not a vertical superior of any other person, nor can it apply to the Judges of the Supreme Court and for that matter even to the Supreme court Judges. [620B] 1.2 The words in clause (e) have to be given some meaning which would place the burden on the prosecution, howsoever light, to make out a prima facie case for obtaining sanction of the competent authority under Section6(1)(c) of the Act and this can be done only if the alleged misbehaviour is connected with his office. [720C] 1:3 The words "any other person" in clause(e) are clear pointer in the direction that the Parliament has not as yet considered it expedient to enact any such law for the trial and punishment on the charge of corruption of a superior Judge instead of the general law. [821B] 2.4 The words used in clause 5(e), have to take their colour from the scheme of which the Public servant is sought to be inferred, and not to the Chief Justice or the ChiefJustice exercising only moral authority over his colleagues in the Supreme Courts and the High Courts, much less the Supreme Curt Judges: The incumbent of the office of Chief Justice, exercising only administrative power over his subordinates in the manner provided in Article 124(5) as the only punishment; and a special law enacted by the Parliament under Article 124 (5), even for investigation and proof of any misbehaviour alleged against a superior judge instead of general law was clearly visualised when the alleged misbehavior is connected to his office, [721C] 2:5. The words 'any other persons' in clause 4(1) (c) have been given some significance which would include the Chief Justices and Judges, who are not members of that House, much higher than the Supreme Judge or the High curt Judges. It is for this reason that the Legislature has not made any provision which cannot apply to a Judge holding such office. The fact that the legislature did not enact any other law even then for the investigation into allegations of corruption against a subordinate Judge and for his trial and punishments for that offence and rest content merely with enacting the , to provide for the procedure for remov al of a Judge under Article124(4) is a clear pointer to the direction, that the President of India may be deemed to be the authority to grant sanction in accordance with the procedure envisaged in Article124 (5) read with Article 2 18. [758G] 3:6 The words of clause (ee) have not been given any meaning which could possibly apply to Judges of High Court Judges, since the Chief Judge of India exercises only moral power over their colleagues in a Supreme Court or theHigh Court Judges. The mere fact that a Parliament did not provide for any special law would not make out any prima facie Case for obtaining sanctions under Section 5(1).

The appellant was a member of the Scheduled Caste specified in item 40 of the Schedule Caste. He challenged the election on the ground that he belonged to a smaller group of Sunri caste which had nothing to do with Sunri and that it was, therefore, not open to him at the trial to contend that the Sahas were originally a smaller caste group within the Sunri community. The Tribunal held that item 40 included Sahas in Schedule Caste specified therein but did not claim, by virtue of abundant caution, so that the appellant bore the surname Saha holding that item40 excluded Sahas from Sunri. The High Court set aside the order of the Tribunal and directed the election of the appellant to be set aside on the grounds that the respondent belonged to an independent caste which was a smaller one. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent (i) that the word 'Saha ' in item 41 meant "a person belonging to a larger group" and not a member thereof, and (ii) that there was no evidence before the Tribunal that the said Sahas formed a sub caste within the meaning of item 40. HELD: (1) The word ' Saha ' in the expression 'excluding Saha ' is a caste, the word "Saha" in the clause must be read as including Saha ' excluding Saha ' and not merely Saha '. [390 B] (2) In the present case the appellant had established that the sub caste of Sahas was a larger one. The fact that the appel lant belonged to the smaller group called Sahas did not show that there were within the said Sunri, by reason of abundant precaution so that Sahas who bore the traname Saha could claim, without more. [391 C D] (3) In view of the matter, the correct interpretation of item 41 was that Saha's name was a sub Caste and had not been proved to belong to the larger group called 'Saha" within the concept of Sunrri caste.

The appellant was a tenant of the premises in question. The respondent, who was the second respondent in this appeal, entered into negotiations with the complainant for putting him in vacant possession of the flat and an additional amount of Rs. 2,000 was paid to him by the appellant. The appellant agreed to pay the sum of Rs 29,500 to be paid back on the appellant 's return to India. The police party, who were down below ready for the raid, held up the car of the appellant and recovered the sum o f Rs. 29, 500 and he was further charged under section 19(2) of the Act for receiving the said sum as a condition for the relin quishment of his tenancy. The complainant and the Sub Inspec tor, who are down below tire floor, went to the appelant on 4 12 1948, and recovered Rs. 1,000 from the complainant. The complaint was lodged by the respondent against the appellant under section 13(1)(e) of The Indian Penal Code. The Magistrate convicted him under section 20(2), but he convicted him for an offence under section 18(2). On appeal to the High Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the offence arose only on receipt of any sum or any consideration as a condi tion by a tenant o his tenancy and not a relinquishment. Held, that the word "relinquishment" used in the section is not a term of art and is used in its comprehensive sense as giving up possession of property or the giving of his consent by the landlord to the transfer of a lease by sub lease or otherwise on receipt o consideration that has been made an offence. The consent of the landlord, to an assignment is not necessary in the absence of a contract or local usage to the contrary. The word "surrender" used therein is meant, appropriate words could have been used, such as the transfer by a lessee or tenant of his rights as such. The other parts of the order of the learned Presidency Magistrate, as regards the disposal of Rs 1,500 paid by the complainant to the appellant, will, however, stand.

The appellant, who maintained a wage scale of Rs. 150/ and Rs. 100/ in the category of Draftsmen and Rs 150/ in that category of Draughtsman and Rs 200/ in other categories, was entitled to get a flat increase of Rs 150/- in the class of Draftsman and also to pay dearness allowance and there was no mention of giving any ad hoc increase in the basic pay of individual workmen. The appellant maintained that the existing wage scales were fair and reasonable on a region cum industry basis and that it would not be possible for the appellant to bear additional financial burden if the demands of the Union were accepted. The Industrial Tribunal, however, held that the revised wage scales had necessarily to commence with figures Rs.150/ and that there was nothing in the body of the award to form the foundation on which the actual figures in the restructured pay scales could be made to rest. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the Union that the expression "flat increase" occurring in section 2(k) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, means a change in the existing conditions of service and not an alteration in the conditions of services of the employees. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The word "filter increase" is used in the sense that it includes a change of conditions of employment or change of condition of service. [176C] 2. The expression "instead of any work or class of workmen" in section 3(k), means an alteration of conditions and conditions of work, which is not intended to be altered by the employer. It is only when there is a change that the conditions are changed by the employee. In the instant case, the Industrial Tribunal had merely revised the wage scales by increasing the salary on entry into the service and res 184 tructuring the scale of pay and never granted any adhoc increase in salary to all employees. The omission of the words to each employee first after the figure Rs. 200/ and again after the figures were Rs. 151/ and thereafter after the word figure Rs 150 / was added to the pay of every other workman, who belonged to the Union staff, the financial load would increase to Rs. 50/ in addition to the existing wages scales. Immediately after the award was pronounced, while the iron was still hot as it were, the employees apparently realised that the employer might take advantage of the circumstance that it was not clearly mentioned in the award that all the employees were to get additional pay of Rs, 150/ or Rs.100/ respectively and might contend that the Tribunal had only revised the wages by increasing its salary on Entry into the Service and never granting any ad adhoc increase of salary to All employees. [177D E] 3. The words "in stead of anything done in pursuance of this award" occurring therein, mean an alteration or change in conditions of labour or service or change or condition of work which is necessary for the proper implementation of the provisions of the Act. [178C D] 4. In making the award dated December 20, 1978 the Tribunal was betrayed by a curious confusion in accepting the plea of the appellant that a flat increased to the Pay of each individual workman was intended in the original wage and, consequently, it fell into the error of amending the award. The omissions of the word "Filter increases" are clearly intended by the Tribunal as is evident from the reference to "fat increase of pay". [177E F] 5. The appellant was employed as a driver in the respondent company. The respondents were paid wages at the rate of Rs. 250 per day. The appellant paid its employees only As. / 10 / 10/ per day and that led to the present claim made by the respondents under section 15 of the Act. The employer contended before the authority that the refusal of the appellant to pay to them wages at a rate awarded in substance amounted to an illegal deduction from their wages and on that basis they asked for an order from the authority directing the appellant, to pay the said prescribed wages. Held, that the terms prescribed by an award could not be included. The terms prescribed in an award, in law, constitute a fresh contract between the parties, because that, in substance, is the effect of industrial adjudication. That being so, it is difficult to accede to the argument that even under the unamended definition of wages, rates of remuneration prescribed by the award could also not be excluded. It was then well settled that where an award made by an Industrial Tribunal cannot be said to amount to a contract of employment, the wage structure prescribed by it must be deemed to be a contract between employers and workmen make it reasonable to think that even though the period of operation of the award and the period for which it remained binding on the parties may elapse in respect of both of which special provisions have been made under sections 23 and 29 respectively the new contract would continue to govern the relations between the employer and the employees. The words " wages" in section 2(vi) of the , must be read as including wages directed to be paid by industrial adjudication, and since an award passed by an industrial tribunal cannot be treated as wages under section 2 (vi), it is not open to the Industrial Court to interfere with that award.

The appellant was a Sub Divisional Officer in the Public Works Department, Pepsu. He was prosecuted under section 409 of the Indian Penal Code for having committed certain works at a place called Karhali. The trial Magistrate convicted him both under section 465 and section 409 I.P.C. and sentenced him to one year 's rigorous imprisonment. On appeal by the State to the High Court, the appellant contended that sanction was necessary under section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure for prosecution under section misappropriation of funds and that there having been an acquittal of the appellant by the trial Magistrate, the materials on record did not justify a reversal of that verdict by the appellate Court. Held: (i) The prosecution which has resulted in the conviction of the accused was initiated without sanction under section 196(1). The charge against him was framed without any sanction under s 197(2) of Code of Civil Procedure and if sanction under that section is necessary, as contended for by Mr. According to the respondent, however, the main charge against the appellant was under section 408 I. P.C., and no sanction was required for a prosecution under that Section. (ii) The mere fact that the accused did not pay the amount to Parma, and the acquittance roll records the payment, and there is in acknowledgment thereof a thumb impression as against his name. If what appears on the face of the roll is true and whether it is true or not is not a matter relevant at the stage of sanction then the acts with which the appellant is charged fall within the scope of his duties, and can be justified by him as done by virtue of his office. (iii) The sanction was not necessary under s. 197(l) of Criminal P. C., for prosecution of the person doing it, that he could not, when charged with it, claim justification for it by virtue Of his office, that therefore no sanction under the section was necessary and that the question was concluded by the decisions in Hori Ram Singh vs Emperor (1) and Albert We8 Meads vs The King (2), in both of which the charges were of criminal misappropriation.

The assessee was a resident of Travancore State in the erstwhile State of Cochin. The income tax authorities included the profits of the business and assessed them to income tax under section 12B of the Travancore Income tax Act, Travancore. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the business losses incurred in the former State could be set off against the business profits made in British India or Travancore State as the case may be. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the first proviso to section 24(1) of the Indian Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1941, did not apply to the present case because the word " income" used in the proviso to sub section (2) of section 14 of the Act did not include business losses which were incurred in British country or in an Indian State and that the words " loss of profits or gains arising from him within the meaning of clause (e) of sub section(2) Of section 18 of the Income tax, 1922, were used in relation to business or vocation carried on by a resident outside India. Held, that the mere use of the words loss of profit or gains to be, set off under section 10 must mean business in British Indian States only and not to any other section. The mere fact that the word ' income " is not used does not justify the construction. that the intention of the Legislature was to restrict the set off of profits and losses arising under the head business in the two territories, i. e., British India and the Indian States.

The Company challenged the validity of an agreement entered into between the Company and its employees at Calcutta under which the age of retirement was extended to 58 years subject to the employees passing a medical examination on reaching the age Of 55. The Tribunal held that in all the awards in recent times there was no uniform trend in Bombay region to fix the retirement age at 60, that is, between 1952 and 1961, that the trend in the Bombay region had been to fix retirement age of clerical and subordinate staff at 60 years subject only to the employee passing a Medical examination on reaches the age o 55. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the workmen that the decision of the Tribunal in dealing with this aspect of the problem was erroneous, because it was not correct to say that the error committed by the Tribunal was in fact inaccurate and was therefore liable to be set aside. HELD: The Tribunal had found that in Bombay the trend had been about fixing the retirement ages at 60 and that its present conclusion that what was said by itself on an earlier occasion and was confirmed by this Court in appeal, was on the whole unsound. [446B] In all the cases the age was fixed at 60. On a consideration of all the facts and circumstances disclosed by the oral and documentary evidence on this record, we are satisfied that the Tribunal had not committed any error in fixing the age for retirement at 60; and that it was rightly held that the conclusion recorded by this court in some of its earlier decisions as to the relevant trend in this case was erroneous. [546C] The Tribunal has failed to notice that in the Calcutta region there is a general agreement with regard to the age and retirement of the workmen 's case that the recent trend in Madras region had not been to fixing the superannuation age at 58 subject to certain exceptions which had been introduced by agreement for the Bombay employees retirement at the ageof 55. [646B C] The very few departures from this practice which the Tribunal has mentioned are, in our opinion, wholly insufficient to indicate any slowing down of this trend. What the Tribunal have failed to notices is that instances which may justify a revision of the judicial opinion expressed on an previous occasion about a particular trend must be strong and unambiguous and they must speak for the period both before and more particularly after the previous finding had been recorded in the matter. 429 The very many departuresfrom this practice, which the tribunal has mentioned were, in my opinion, totally insufficient to show any slowness down of that trend must have been strong and categorical and they should speak forthe period bothbefore and more especially after the earlier finding hadbeen recorded in its matter. 430 The Tribunal was therefore justified in interfering with the award fixing the date of retirement at 58 years.

The appellants were the managing agents of M/s Barium Chemicals Ltd. and M/S Barium Chemical Works Ltd., who were directors of M. P. Industries Ltd. The first respondent was the managing agent of M P. Industrial Corporation Ltd. (the appellant) and the second respondent was its managing agent. The second respondent passed an order under section 237(b) of the Act directing the appellants to appoint one or more competent persons as inspectors to investigate the affairs of the company and to report thereon in such manner as the Central Government may direct. The appellants challenged the validity of the said order on the ground that it was not competent to pass an order in exercise of its power under section 240(b). Held, that the discretion conferred on the Central Board by section 237 (b) to order an investigation and delegated by it to the Company Law Board is administrative, that it could be validly exercised by the Chairman of the Board by an order made in pursuance of a rule enacted by the Central Legislature under section 642(1) read with section 10E(5), that the exercise of the power does not violate any fundamental right of the appellants and its members. The power conferred on a Central Government by section 238(b), to order investigation and delegate by it, is administrative; that it can be validly delegated by the Board but it has no power to authorise the Chairman to sub delegate this function to himself and consequently, the Company law Board (Procedure) Rules, 1964 made by the State Government on February 6, 1964 and the Chairman 's order of distribution of business dated February 6 1964 delegating the functions of the board under section 239 to the Chairman are ultra vires the and the impugned order is invalid.

The appellants were tried and convicted for the same offence and received a like sentence. The trial court acquitted them under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code but reduced their sentences to one year ' rigorous imprisonment. On appeal by special leave, the High Court set aside the conviction and sentence of the appellants. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the presumption in the case of dacoity was established because dacoity was proved; (ii) the fact that the accused were dacoits would not have been sufficient to bring home the charge under section 411 of the Code, and (iii) the prosecution had failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the appellants were dacoits. HELD : The conviction was correct in all the circumstances of the case. It is only when the accused can be connected with the crime itself that the presumption may be drawn under section 114 of the Evidence Act but not have the lesser presumption. [723 B] (i)(ii) In the present case, the appellants had been convicted on the sole evidence of having in their possession pieces of cloth which were later identified to belong to the traders. The presumption was stronger when the discovery of the stolen goods was made immediately after the crime is made immediately before the offence. [823 C] (iii)(iv) In some cases there may be other elements which may be found, but small, the finding of the theft property with a particular accused. It must not be forgotten that in some cases it may be possible to think that within the short time available, these goods could have been easily disposed of receivers of stolen property or could be placed in the custody of friends till such time as the original offenders could take them away. [825 E] (v) The presumption under section 412 of the Criminal Procedure Code is not a rule of law but it is only a rule that the burden of proof lies on the accused to prove his innocence. In this case, there was no other evidence to show the complicity of the persons in the crime.

The expression "polysenic", the expanded words are used in a sense similar to those used in the Act, and the object of which is to control the poss ession thereof desirable, is to render provision for regulating the possession of any specified poison in any local area in which it is intended for use as an ingredient of murder or other offence. [225E F] 4. The notification and its application to any area would depend on the necessity to declare the substance which it considers to be poison for purpose of committing death or mischief, by poisoning. If Government thought that the possess ment or sale was to be governed in the interest of health and safety of the society, it could have no such power to control. [226F G] 5. The Notification and its appli cation to any other area would not depend on necessity to declaring the substance ance as poison. [227G] 6. The Government may by rule regulate the import, Possession and sale or sale to be regulating the possibil ity for sale or disposal of the specified poison. It is in exercise of this power Rule 13 was amended by substituting the old Rule by following Rule 13. [228H; 227A B] 7. The State Government may, by rule regulating the import or possession of potions, possession etc., which shall be kept within such box, almirah, room or building in a separate closed receptacle of glass, metal and earthenware etc. The nature of trade in poison is such that nobody can be considered to have an absolute right to carry on the same. [229C D; 228D] 8. The notifications and the application to the any area will depend on whether the substance was specified as a poison or not. If it is found that the Government has no power under the Act to regulate, the possession for sale and the sale of such an article would be governed by Rule 12. [230E F; 228F] 9.

The assessee firm applied to the Tribunal under section 66(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 for referring the following question to the High Court: "Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, the Tribunal was right in law in holding that the debt of Rs. 2,68,385/ written off as irrecoverable in the books of account was not one incurred in the course of money lending business of the assessee ?" The Tribunal rejected the application but pursuant to an order made by the High court under section 67(2) submitted a statement of the cases on the following questions " Whether on the findings and in law, the Income tax Officer was right In law in disallowing the debt. " HELD : (i) The debt in question was not a bad and doubtful debt in its money lending trade or business nor a debt representing loss sustained in the other business. [12 E] (ii) The Tribunal has found that the monies sent by the assessee to the Bombay firm were not loans made in the ordinary course of their money lending, but in respect of any other business of assessee. It is true that the amounts sent by them to the Madras firm were neither loans made nor in respect thereof. [13 E F] (iii) The amount sent by it to the Calcutta firm was not loans advanced in the normal course of its moneylending business nor in regard to any other income of the appellant. [14 G H] (iv) The amounts sent to the Delhi firm were never loans made, but only in respect o loans made by that firm in the usual course of the money lending businesses. It was not an "accommodation" account to enable the Bombayfirm to tide over the "financial crisis". [15 E F].

The petitioners were owners of certain lands which were acquired by the respondents under the provisions of the Bangalore Development Act, 1976. The Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1984 was brought into force on September 20, 1977. The petitioners obtained an interim order from this Court directing status quo with regard to the possession of the lands in question in Special Leave Petition No. 294 of 1985 preferred against the said order of the High Court dated August 14, 1984. The said special leave petition was dismissed by a Division Bench of that High Court on April 29, 1987. In these two writ petitions, the petitioners challenged the acquisition on the ground that they were not made within two years of the notification making the declaration under section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. Dismissing the Special Leave Petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The fact of the stay orders was highly material in the determination of these Special Leave petitions. [565E] 2. The question whether the awards were made within the stipulated time or not is a matter which has to be decided by the court on the basis of the evidence and materials placed before it. [567F] 3. In the instant case, the respondents have failed to make out any case for interference with the acquisition proceedings. [568G] 4. The Special Leave Petitioners are approaching this Court for such relief must come with clean hands. They have not approached this Court with clean hand and they have not suppressed material facts. [569F] 5. The High Court has granted interim stay of dispossession in respect of the said lands. It is well settled that the relief under Article 136 of the Constitution is discretionary and a petitioner who approaches this Court seeking such relief should come with frank and full disclosure of facts. If he fails to do so and suppresses material facts, his application is liable to be dismissed. [570F] 6. The order granting interim stay is not a direction for continuance of the proceedings till the disposal of the Special leave petition. It does not amount to suppression of material facts or there was no concealment of material fact. [571G H] 7. The petitioner has failed to show that the stay order was made within time. If the respondents appeared in response to the notice and filed their counter affidavit, they have failed in their defence. They are liable to pay compensation for the delay caused by them. [573F G] 8.

The appellant bank was a nationalised bank. The workmen were drawing basic pay at the rate of Rs. 250 per month. The Sastry award provided that the workmen would be fitted in the new scales of pay from January 1, 1962 on stage to stage adjustment basis, i.e., workmen who entered service of the bank before 1st January 1959 shall not be reduced in any case. The appellant bank filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the award and also the validity or otherwise of the Sastry award. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Sastry Award provided that "the workmen would work in the old scales of Rs 250 per year as on January 1 1959, and that they would be entitled to increments under sub cl. (a) of cl. 182. Held, that the High court was right in holding that it had no jurisdiction to entertain the writ application. The award provided for a revision of the existing scales of dearness allowance and the revision of pay scale. The revision of scales of Dearness Allowance and the revisions of pay scales were not governed by the Sastry Awards Award. The Desai Award provided for revision of existing scales and the revised pay scale was to be fixed as on February 1, 1959. The scheme of the Desai award was that the scales of allowances in the existing grades would be revised from time to time. The variation in the scales was not a matter of course. It was only with reference to the scales which were earlier fixed by the Desai Award. There was no provision for revision and it was not open to the Sastry Tribunal to revise the scales. The present case was covered by cl. 5. (ii) of the National Industrial Tribunal (Bank Disputes) Award, the adjusted basic pay in the revised scale was not to exceed what point to point adjustment would give an employee on January1, 1959, as modified by placing him at the stage in the Sastry awards scale equal to or next above his basic pay as on 1st February 1959.

The appellants, who were the owners of four acres of land in Calcutta, applied for a lease of the Begumbari land to the respondent No. 1 on February 12, 1981. The respondent No, 1 was granted a lease by the Government of West Bengal on February 13, 1981 and the respondent Nos. 2 and 3 were granted a licence for the construction of Five Star Hotel. On March 12,1981, the respondent no. 1 filed an application before the State Government under section 5(1) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') seeking permission to sell the Begambari land in question. The State Government rejected the application on the ground that the lease was not a licence and that the respondent had no locus standi to file the application. On appeal by the appellants, the Division Bench held that the decision taken was neither unreasonable nor arbitrary and that taking away of four acre of land from the Zoo for the purpose of encouraging setting up industries within the State, the Government was quite alive to the need for expan sion of the zoo for a single day without the essential services which were being provided in the four acres o f land proposed to be given for the hotel. The appellants filed an appeal before this Court against the decision of the Division bench. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The State would have to auction or invite tenders for securing the highest price, subject, of course, to any other relevant overriding considerations of public interest. But in a case like this where the State is allo cating resources such as water, power raw materials etc. for the purposes of encouraging set up of industries within th State, we do not think the State would be justified in proceeding on the basis that the land which was undoubt edly Government land, to start with, was given to the Zoological Garden upon the terms set out in the two letters. [623B] 1.2 The State is bound to advertise and tell the people that it wants a particular industry to be set up within the state and invite those interested to come up with pro posals for thepurpose of encouraging sets up of Industries within the States and invite them for the Purpose of encouraging Set up of units within the Zoogical Garden. [723C] 1:3 The State has made available to this Court all documents in connection with the proposal for lending over a piece of the State Govt. land to respondent No 1. The matter was taken in appeal. [761D] 2.1 In the face of the assurance of the Chief Minister that facilities would be provided for the Zillogical Garden, upon the Terms set out therein, we are satisfied that the construction o f the pro posed hotel in Calcutta was given tapping contract simpliciter there can be no doubt that what is involved here is not the sale of the land but a lease for the construc tion of a Five Star hotel in Delhi. [764A] 2:2 The Government was very alive to this need for Expan sions which were having weighed with the Government in taking a particular action, that the Court would haveto decide whether the action of the Government is reasonable and in public interest; but in a cating circumstance like this when the State has taken an appropriate decision, that it wanted a particular Industry to be Set up within th e State and invite such persons interested to coming up with Pro posals. [765B] 3.1 It is on a total evaluation of various considerations which have weighed with tapping contracts simpliciter there could be no question of any resin being sold in the open market.

The assessee, a partnership firm, carried on money lending business in the name of his son. The Income Tax Officer held that the sum of Rs.67,560/12 was rightly included in the net wealth of the assessee. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that it was not necessary to make any gifts aggregating to the amount gifted to the donee and gift in such case would not constitute delivery over the gifted property to the donor and gift could not be valid. The High Court also held that there was no valid gift on the date of the entries, and that the assessee did not make any valid gifts aggregating Rs.1,50,000. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the assessee that the amount of Rs.,67, 560/12 could not constitute a valid gift because the assessee had made a valid gifts of Rs 1 lakh and Rs.50, 000 in his favour and the gift of Rs 25,000 made in his name and the gifted of Rs 50,000 was rightly excluded from the net assets of the assesses. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High Courts were right in holding that the amounts gifted to a donee would not form part of the property passing on the death of the donor. [130D] (2) The assessee had a credit amount with firm or with family or with a banking company and that sum was available to that firm or company which carried on moneys lending business also. It was held on the facts of that case that there were no valid gifts worth Rs. 1,50 ,000 made by the deceased to his son and to his wife respectively. [131E] (3) The gift was held to be invalid because the amount was not available with the firm or the family or a company which was not a banking Company or which had no overdraft facility by mere book entries might be possible but where a sum was not present with the family, then a valid Gift by book entry might be reasonably possible but when a sum is not available to the firm, it resulted in a valid transfer even though there was acceptance of that gift by the donee would effectuate a valid purchase. [132F] (4) The fact that the money was transferred by further entries in the books of account of the firm would not make no difference because the transaction was genuine and there was an agreement to sell. [134G] (5) The amount gifted was not received back by the donor but was credited in the personal account of his wife, and the gifts were held to have been made contemporane ously shown that the transaction had been made Yours propor tive.

The appellant was appointed as a district judge in the Orissa High Court on October 10, 1966. He was transferred to the Orissa Administrative Tribunal by an order dated October 10 1966. The appellant challenged his transfer before the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that those officers had no authority to act as law secretary, superintendent and legal remembrance and member sales tax tribunal respectively on and after October 10. 1966 and (2) commanding the State Government to send back judicial officers working in administrative posts as district judges or as addl. district judges as the case may be, after they had held those posts for three years or more. The State appealed to this Court by special leave. HELD: (1) The High Courts were within its powers in posting Shri B.K. Panda as the law secretary of the Orissa high Court and the High court. [628 C] (2)(a) The rule laid down in that decision is of no assistance in determining the question as to whether the High Courts have power to fill up some of the posts in the secretariat. If this be the meaning, as the High High Court holds. then the transfer of District Judges already appointed or promoted and posted in the cadre must necessarily be outside the power of the Governor and fall to be made by the High courts as part of the control vested in it by article 235. [613 D E] (b) The order of the High 'Court posting Shri K.B. Panda was not a law secretary but an administrative remembrancer and member sale tax tribunal, respectively on or after October 12, 1966 and therefore could not be said to be vitiated. [529 G H] (3)(a). The High court was within its jurisdiction in posting the appellant as the Law Secretary, Shri B,K. Bose and Shri P.K.. But as mentioned earlier, the government had already implemented that part of that order as well. In the result these appeals are partly allowed and the order of High Court holding that Shri B was not the law Secretary, deputy law secretary and superintendent and Legal remembheat and Shri K,B.Mishra as superintendent and judicial remembraint and member Sales tax tribunal were included in the Cadre, the High Curt was within their powers in transferring Shri B to the State of Orissa. [625 G H; 627 A] (4) The transfer of a District Judge already appointed and promoted and posting in the cadres must necessarily mean that he is transferred from one post to another. If the High Judge holds that as the posts of the law clerk, deputy Law Secretary and superintendent are included in cadre, the State government or the High' Court has the power to recall them and post them as presiding officers of district courts.

The appellant, a co sharer, was the vendor of the respondent 's brother. The respondent ' s brother had purchased land from his father and mother in the year 1962. The sale deed was executed on 12th January, 1963. The appellant filed an application under section 15(1)(a) of the Punjab Preemption Act, 1913 for pre emption of the appellant 's son 's sons 's daughters 's daughter 's sister 's brothers and brother 's father 's mother 's husband. The trial court held that there was no infringement of Article 19(1) (f) of Constitution. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court upheld the constitutional validity of clause 'fourthly ' and 'fifthly ' of section 15 of the Act. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The expression 'other co sharers ' in section 15 (1)(b) of Punjab Pre preemptionemption Act refers to only those co shars who do not fail under clause 'Fourthly ' or 'Secondly '. [515E] 2.2 In the instant case also the suit land belonged to more than one co sharter and had not been sold jointly by all the co sharters. The expression "other cosharers" in section 14(1A)(b), is meant to serve as a residuary clause to ensure 127 that, no co sharker is left out. [615B] 3.2 The legislature desired to confer the right of pre emation on specified family members of the vendor or vendors who were specified in the erstwhile first three clauses of section 14 (1A) and with a view to covering all the remaining co sharts not specifically mentioned the preceding clauses it used the expression 'Other co sharERS ' in the fourth clause which was meant to serving as a special clause to ensuring 127 that no cosharer is leftout. [715C] 3:3 The legislature wanted to confer a right of preemption on certain relatives or relatives of the vendors who are specified in those erstwhile first two clauses of Section 15(2)(b). It desired to give a benefit to those relative or relatives who were not specified in that clause. [815E H; 816A] 4.4 The legislature intended to confer an additional right on certain relative or relative of the purchaser or vendors, who are not specified therein. [917F] 5.5 In the context, it becomes clear that the legislature desired that no Co sharer is left to out. Hence, the object of clause "fourthly" in clause 'Thirdly ' in clause (b) was to deny the right to hold, acquire or dispose of property conferred by Article 19 (1)(f) and clause fourthly of section15(1). [816B] 6.6 The expression ''other cosharer' in clause "Fourthly" refers to all the members of a family who do either fail under clauses 'Second or 'Thirdally or 'Firstly or 'firstly or secondly ', respectively. [820C] 7.7 In the present case also, the suit property belonged to one cosharers and had no right of sale or dispose off the land or property sold or a part thereof. The question is whether the intention of the legislature was to confer such a right on the vendor. It is seen that the expression "any co shar er" in Section 14(2) (b), refers to both the cosharers who do neither fail under any of the clauses mentioned in the preceding clause and the father ' or vendors Fourthly, in the other co sharor and the tenants can exercise the right conferred on them by that provision.

The petitioner, who was the son of one of the sons of the first respondent, filed a suit for title and injunction. The trial court decreed the suit on the ground that the compromise deed was not genuine and lawful and the alienees had no intention to accept the compromise. In appeal, the High Court held that once the Court was satisfied that there was a compromise it was for the Court to record the same and no option lay before the Court under Order 23, Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the face of such a statement in the compromise Deed signed by the parties, the second respondent had disputed the fact of payment and has, therefore, no right to claim mesne profits. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the alienee that the alienation was valid and binding and the transferees have become owners of the property prior to the compromise and they even maintained that there were agreements for sale prior to 21.8.1987. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court has rightly held that the alienations are valid and the transfers have becomeowners of the properties by the alienors. [540C] 2.1 In view of the fact that there is a allegation of payment of Rs. 1 lakh to Sudarshan Gupta which we have not investigated and to meet the further allegation that some improvements have been made to the property which too we have never gone into, it is unnecessary to refer to the facts leading to the litigation. [541D] 2:2 The alienees have admittedly been in possession of the land from the date of the sales which is more than three years old by now. In fact if the compromise is valid and enforceable the alienor respondent No. 2 had no interest in the property to part with in view of his stipulation in the agreement that on receipt of Rs, 1 lakh each and the second and third respondents have received the same. The alienee has not been able to point out any justification as to why the compromise should not be acted upon and on the basis of it the litigation may not be disposed of. [542C D] 2 :3 In view Of the fact the suit is genuine and valid, the same has to be acted on. [543D] 3:4 The alienes shall deliver vacant possession of his property by 30th April, 1991, to Seshiah and in the event of failure to do so the Trial Court is directed by our present order to deliver vacant physical possession of that property in suit including those which are covered by the sale deeds in favour of the transferees to Seshaah within one month therefrom. If necessary, the Trial court may appoint a Commissioner and take police help for executing this order and such cost shall ultimately be borne by the defaulting alienees but may initially be met by the concerned alienees and then be met from the defaulting vendees.

The workmen of the Company were granted sick leave for 7 days sick leave on full pay and dearness allowance in 1958 subject to the condition that the benefit would cease to apply when the benefits of the Employees ' State Insurance Scheme would become available to the workmen. The workmen, however felt aggrieved because of the first proviso to section 49 of the , filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the award on the ground that the Tribunal had given the benefit of sick leave and that the workmen did not deserve any relief for the first two days of sickness except in the case of a spell of sickness following, at an interval of not more than 15 days. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the benefits admissible under the Act in the matter of grant of sick Leave are such as to justify the rejection of the workmen 's demand and the setting aside of the Tribunal 's awards in that respect. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High court had not given any reasons for allowing the benefit to the sick leave with retro spective effect from January 1, 1975 in view of the second proviso to Section 49 of The Act and that since the Tribunal has corrected under a mistaken impression of the sickness benefit which the Act allowed for as has been shown, it does not deal with all aspects of the demand for sickness benefit and did not, at any rate, provide for the grant of leave on Full emoluments during the period of the workman 's physical incapacity to earn his normal wages because of his sickness. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The Tribunal has committed an error in allowing the relief to the workman. [864C] 2.1 In the instant case, the Tribunal was under a misconception that 86 the sickness benefits would be lost for the second two days also. It is not necessary that in the circumstances of the case, to award the benefit, the sick Leave with retro grative effect should cease to applied when the benefit is last paid. [874D] 2:2 The Tribunal had correctly examined the matter and given adequate reasons for awarding the benefit. Such a leave could not be categorised as privilege leave as, by its very nature, it would be admissible only in the cases of actual sickness certified by a registered medical practitioner. It appears, however, that it was not necessary, in the facts of the present case to award benefit of the sick leaves with retro modtive effect on January 1 1975 in the garb of sick. [884E F] 2 :3 The Tribunal ' has cor rectly considered the controversy and given sufficient reasons for granting the benefit under 7 days Sick leave in the manner set out in the award. Such leave could be treated as privilege Leave as, By its very nomenclature, it is not a privilege leave. It was not permissible to give any reason for allowing sick leave without retro specious effect from time to time. [894G H] 2(a) The Tribunal should have given the benefits under 7 months sick leave in view Of the fact that the company had cor rected under the mistaken impression that 86 sickness benefit would be loss for the 1st two days. It has also correatedly examined whether the workmen were entitled to any of the benefits provided by the Act, and give adequate reasons therefor. Such an leave could only be categorised in the category of actual illness certified by registered medical practitioners. [904G] 2.(b) The High court was not justified in allowing a benefit of 7 days sickness leave as it would amount to granting privilege leave on half emoluments during that period of his physical incapacity.

The appellant was an Advocate of the High Court of Bombay. He had a standing of about thirty years. The grounds were not vague or not, but want of bona fides, as well as the non application of mind, on the part of the detaining authority, viz., the Government, which for this purpose must be taken to be different from the police. The High Court dismissed an application made by the appellant under article 226 of the Constitution on the ground that the grounds furnished are vague and not in public interest. On appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the non communication of the decision to disclose facts considered against public interest cannot be said to have hampered his constitutional right of representation, and that the failure of the authority to communicate the decision is fatal to the detention order. Held: (i) The right of the detenue to be furnished particulars, at least to that extent, it will enable him to present to the Advisory Board his difficulties in making a proper representation and to convey to it a request for obtaining the requisite particulars from the State under section 10 of the Act for their own information and consideration. But in the absence of any such request by the detenue, the non Communication of the order decision cannot be held to have adversely affected his constitutional rights of representation. The right to be supplied particulars, is subject to the limitation under article 22(6) whereby disclosure of facts considered to be against public interests cannot be implied in these circumstances. If the appellant bad exercised his right to ask for particulars at the time when the grounds were furnished, there can be no doubt that he would have been furnished then the very information which has been supplied in paragraph 12 of the Under Secretary 's affidavit and there is nothing to suggest that this question was not considered by the detaining Authority at the relevant time when it was made. The non communication, therefore, cannot be construed as having hampered the constitutional right to representation. [723C D] (ii)The right of a detenue to make a representation is subject only to the limitations under article 19(6), and not to any restriction on the exercise of the power by the authority concerned. The obligation to communicate cannot be inferred in these cases having regard to the nature of the 393 grounds on which the detention is based and the nature thereof, as was pointed out by this court in the State of Bombay vs Atma Ram Sridhar Vaidya(1) in the following passage: "The right to make representation is a constitutional right. The power not to disclose information considered against Public interest cannot therefore be implied In these circumstances, it can only mean that the right of an detenue to have access to the relevant material at the place where the detention was based and his personal knowledge or belief are likely to be affected by the prejudicial activities carried on by him." [724C D; 723A B] (iii)The non communication is not in a public interest to disclose the details of the activities alleged to have been carried on so as to nullify the constitutional rights. The question whether or not article 22 (6) of the constitution overrides the constitutional Right to be furnish particulars under article 21(6).

The respondent was a member of the Army Staff. He was dismissed from service on the ground that he had been convicted by a General Court Martial, and that the action taken thereunder was without authority. The Central Government directed removal from service of Capt. section K. Rao under r. 14 of the Indian Rules 1954. The Chief of the Air Staff, after going through the proceedings of the Court of Inquiry, considered that the trial of the officer by a general Court Martial was inexpedient and he ordered administrative action to be taken under r, 14 of Army Rules, 1954. On April 9, 1959, an order was passed removing the respondent from service. Rao thereupon filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of removal from the service on grounds inter alia that r.14 of the Defence Rules, 1955, was ultra vires the , and that he should be dismissed from the services. The High Court allowed the petition holding that r 14 of Defence Rules 1954, was intra vires the . Held, that the words "subject to the provisions of this Act" occurring in section 19 makes it clear that there must be rules, and subject to the provision of the Act, such rules, the Central Government may dismiss or remove from the serv ice. The two sections 19 and 45 of the , are mutually exclusive. 14 Of the Army Rules 1954 is not ultra vires. It was argued that the expression "subject" occurring therein in section19 makes section 19 subject to section 45, and the Central Govern ment has thus no power to remove a person from the Service in derogation of the provisions Of section 45. The words "Subject to the other provisions of the . Act and such rules , the Central Govt may dismiss, or remove" in section 21 of the read with r. 15 of the Rules are not ultra Art. 14.

The appellant company was carrying on the business of manufacturing tea. The Company had to pay octroi duty in accordance with r. 21, and the rules relating to that tax or fee by beat of drum in the village and by means of a notice affixed in the office of the Panchayat and at the village chavdi or chora, specifying a date not earlier than one month after the date of such publication, on or after which the panchayat shall take the proposal into consideration. The appellant company filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of r. 22, but the High court dismissed it. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the rules prescribing the procedure for levying tax or fees and were not confined to octroi duty only. Held: (i) that the Standing Committee inspected the premises of the Company but in their order they have given very scanty facts, They do not say whether the tea is crushed, processed or treated chemically to convert it into a marketable commodity. The Standing Committee visited the premises and found that the formalities contemplated by law were complied with. (ii) that these things are done and that the resultant product was completely different from the tea imported into octroi limits. In the present case the Standing committee inspected the building of the company but in its order they had given very Scanty particulars, They did not say what the requirements of law were fulfilled. The rules prescribing procedure for imposing tax or Fee and are not confined only to octroi duties only. (iii) that it enjoins that the procedure prescribed in r. 3 should be followed before the octroi duty can be levied from the date specified in the notice and he says that if the octroi limits had not been approved of by the time the resolution was passed, how could the tax be levied therefrom.

The appellant No. 1 was prosecuted under section 31(1) read with section 33(1)(b) of the , and was convicted by the Chief Presidency Magistrate, Bombay, and sentenced to a fine of Rs. 5 to a sum of Rs, 1 (now appellant No 1) and its Manager H. The appellants challenged their conviction before the High Court under section 32(1), read with sections 33(2)(b), 34(1). The High Court dismissed the appeal but confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that as the conciliation proceedings had continued for a period of more than 14 days as from January 17, 1952, further proceedings for conciliation were illegal and therefore the appellants could not be convicted under section31(1); (i) that the dismissal could not have been said to be one within the words " pendency of conciliation proceedings ". Held: (i)(a) The provisions of section 33 are mandatory in character and they cannot be construed as directory. It is true that section 12 contemplates the submission of the report by the Conciliation Officer within 14 days but that does not affect the pendency of the conciliation proceeding and if for some reason the Conciliation officer delays the submission or his action (1) ; No doubt section 12 envisages that the report should be made and the proceedings closed within a fortnight and if proceedings are not carried on, as they were in the present case, or if the Conciliation Officers do not make their report within 14 day he may be guilty of breach of duty but in law the proceedings do not automatically come to an end after 14 days. The provisions Of section 12(6) of The Act clearly contemplate the submission by the conciliation officer within 14 months and if that report is received by the appropriate Government, the proceedings are closed. [723 C] (ii)The provisions of sections 33 and 34 are mandatory and they do not support this contention as the termination of the Conciliation proceedings is deemed to take place when the report under section 12 is made by the Board but only terminate as provided in section 20(2) (b). The provisions in section 12 are mandatory. They cannot be read as directory, and they can be construed so as to give effect to the intention of the legislature.

The petitioner was detained under section 3(2) of the . The District Magistrate, Dhanbad in respect of the petitioner 's activities were prejudicial to maintenance of public order. The petitioner challenged the detention on various grounds including that he had been falsely implicated and was not at all concerned with the murder; that the detaining authority had confirmed the order of detention without application of mind and without considering the relevant documents referred to and/or relied on, and therefore, the continued detention of the detenu was illegal. The District Judge rejected the petition holding that the petitioner was in jail and was entitled to be released forthwith. In appeal before the High Court it was contended that the order was made on one incident relating to exchange of fire between two rival groups; that there was rational nexus between the object of the order as contemplated by the Act and the materials on record, and that the detention order was necessary for putting him back in jail. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The detaining authority was satisfied that his release from one prison to another was imminent and the order passed was not on proper consideration. [910C] 2. The order of preventive detention could only be justified against a person in custody and there was no possibility of his being released or that there were such a possibility of their release.
