In these circumstances, therefore, while the actual order of the detention was served upon the detenu, the matter of service of the impugned order under the Act on the petitioner and other factors which could justify the detention of a person is in jail, and there is no indication that either the prospect of immediate release or that the prospectof his imminent release was properly considered by the detaining Authority properly and with seriousness consider by the Advisory Board properly and seriously before the service of such order. [1011D E] 3. The detenu has been detained under the Preventive Detention Act, 1950 on the ground that he was in custody of that there had been indiscriminate firing to kill Birendra Pratap Singh a rival of his calendlity business of coal to establish the criminal superiority in full view of the shopkeepers and passers by of the area. [1110F] 4. The detention order passed by the District Magistrate is, therefore set aside. [1211D] 5. The petition is accordingly allowed. The respondents are directed to be set at liberty forthwith.

The appellant, a manufacturer of gold trade, was carrying on business as a money lender or banker on the security of any article, ornament or both in the same premises in which he carried on business. The Administrator granted permission to carry on his business under section 28 of the Gold Control Act, 1968 for the period from 1st April, 1969 to 31st March, 1970. The appellant challenged the validity of section 28 on the ground that it suffers from the vice of excessive delegation of legislative power inasmuch as no criteria or guide lines have been provided by reference to which the power conferred upon the Administrator could be exercised and that the section confers an arbitrary and uncanalised power without any criteria for guiding the discretion of the Administrator. The High Court struck down the aforesaid provision only on the grounds that it suffered from the infirmity of excessive exercise of legislative powers inasmuch as the Administrator had no power to refuse permission or grant permission. In these appeals by special leave, the appellant contended: (1) that section 28 confers an uncanalised and arbitrary power without anything more than any criteria or guidelines for guiding its discretion; (2) that the Administrator is given unlimited authority or power to decline permission or to grant permission; (3) that in making his orders he has regard to the policy and purpose of the Act in making its orders. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The object of putting the Act on the Statute Book as indicated by its long title is "to provide, in the economic and financial interests of the community, for the control of production, manufacture, supply, distribution, use and possession of, and business in, gold ornaments and articles of gold and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto. In other words, the various restrictions that have been put on the activities of the traders doing business in gold will have to be viewed from the aforesaid perspective. [755C D] 1.2 The policy and the scheme of the impugned Act together with the necessity to ensure prevention of circumvention of the other provisions of the Acts afford more than sufficient guidance to the Administrator in the matter of exercising his discretion under that section. [758E F] 1:3 In the absence of parity of situation or circumstances the doctrine of parity cannot be invoked. [759D E] 1 :4. The object and scheme of section 5(1) of the , is to ensure protection of circum potances of the persons engaged in gold trade. It does not impose any blanket or 956 absolute prohibition upon a dealer from carrying on money lending, banking or any other business in the said premises in that premises in connection with which he carries on business in as such dealer. Even the restriction in the case of a third person in carrying on his trade as a dealer but he is prevented only from carrying out business as money lender and while implementing such limited restrictions or granting relief against the same he will be guided by the policy, and purposes of the enactment and by the prime consideration that circumvention Of the other provision of the statute shall not be premitted. [761G H] 1.:5. The objective, the policy & the scheme affords sufficient guidance for the Administrator to exercise his discretion in the matters of exercising the power of discretion conferred on him under section 5 (1). [759E F; 759A B] 2:6. While conferring power on the Administrator under section 4(1), the Administrator was required to have regard to, the anticipated demand, as estimated by him for the ornaments in that region but the expression 'anticipated demand ' was really vague and incapable of assessment leading to a great deal of uncertainty; similarly the expression (1 )AIR 1971 Patna, 240. 112.

The appellants were the owners of agricultural lands situated in Eragudi village, Musiri taluk, Tiruchirappalli district. The properties belonged to the temple and they claimed that they had acquired title by adverse possession prior to 1 1 1929, but on the basis that it was beyond the authority of the manager, the lower appellate Court found that "it was evident that from the very beginning, Pachai Kandai Udayavar and his family had been claiming beneficial interest in the property and they were not holding the same as managers of the trust. The High Court reversed the decision of the trial court and held that "the transfer was effected by the manager as manager purporting to deal with the property as belonging to the religious endowment." In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the question as to whether a transfer effected by an order of the Manager in regard to properties belonging to a religious endowment is void ab initio, and that if the title of the alienees in regard thereto had been acquired by adverse Possession prior to the date of the transfer, it would not be affected by the provisions of article 134 B. Held, further, that the High Court was in error in reversing the decisions of the courts below by holding that the title had not been lost by adverse delivery before the suit was filed. The question as regards whether a sale effected by a manager in regardto properties belonging lo the temple is void, and the decision was based on the facts proved in relation to this aspect of the matter.

The appellant firm was carrying on the business of cinema business in the State of Jammu and Kashmir. The licence for exhibition of cinematographs in the building known as Apsara Theatre, Gandhi Nagar, Jammu was granted by the District Magistrate in favour of the firm. The firm applied to the District Magis trate for a renewal of the licence. The District Magistrate rejected the request on the ground that the licence had been granted to the firm and that it had become impossible for him to operate the Cinema licence in view of the temporary injunction issued by the High Court. The appellant filed an appeal before the State Government against the order of the District magistrate. The State Government dismissed the appeal holding that the renewal of a licence could not be made in the name of any party other than the original licensee, namely, the licensee, who had been declared to be the sole licensee in respect of the Apsar Theatre by the proceedings of his predecessor dated December 29, 1977 which was confirmed in appeal by the State Govt. and which had acquired finality between the parties by reason of the dismissal of the writ petition and the Special Leave Petition by the appellant. The High Court dismissed the writ appeal filed by the firm against the orders of the Sub Divisional Magistrate. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the licensing authority had no power under the Act or the Rules to suspend a licence which could be made only in the names of the original licensees, namely the licensee and there was no mention at all of the partners of the Firm or its partners. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order passed by the Sub Divnt Magistrate directing the suspension of cinema shows in the Theatre cannot be said to have visited the writ petitioners with any adverse civil consequences. [578F] 2. The licensing authority has no power to suspend the licence which can be made under section 6 F of the Act as one implicit in the larger power of revocation and unless the conditions precedent mentioned in the section are present, the licensing authori ty had no jurisdiction to suspend it. [579A B] 3. The only reason stated by the high Court for quashing the District Commissioner 's order is that the District Magistrates had no authority under the . Act or Rules to make such an order. [580C D] 4. The power to suspended a licence is conferred only by section 6F of the , as one implied in the wider power of revoking and unless there is any provision in the Act, the rules framed thereunder cannot be deemed to have been repealed. [581D] 5. The mere fact that the licensee has been declared an insolvent or a person holding an office under him does not by itself make him a party to the proceedings for due compliance with all the terms and conditions of the license and answerable to the licensing authorities for all commissions and omissions in the cinema premises. [583E F] 6.

The appellants, who were the owners of certain mills and the factory in question, applied to the Custodian for cancellation of their lease granted by him under section 12 of the , but the respondent did not give any reply thereto. The Custodian issued a notice to the appellants on 13 2 1954 calling upon them to show cause why they should not be evicted. On 13 2 1951 the appellants appeared before the respondent and contended that he had no auth ority to issue the notice in question under section 10 of the . The Custodian, after considering the objections raised by the appellants, cancelled the lease granted to the appellant on the ground that the appellants had systematically committed breaches of the various terms on which the properties bad been leased to them. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the rights of the appellants in so far as they related to the purchase by them of the mills and factory were left open to the determination of the appropriate authorities, and that under the section as it now stands, the Custodian has the power to cancel leases created not merely by the evacuees but also by himself. The notice in terms refers firstly to the lease which it is proposed to cancel, and secondly to the movables in respect of which certain directions were given. In the present case, the notice was to that extent without juris,diction, and therefore the Custodian had power under section 11 to cancel the agreement to sell the mills. The notices in terms refer firstly to a lease which was in respect for property belonging to the evacuee, that there was no warrant for imposing a further limitation on that section that that lease should also have been granted by the evacuee and not by the Custodian himself, and (2) that the notice, Exhibit C, was to the extent without jurisdiction.

The appellant, a minor son of Raghubir Singh, was born to Raghubir Singh on 14th March, 1963. The ceiling proceedings were finalised by the Sub Divisional Officer on 5th May, 1976 and the Board of Revenue determined the ceiling area for Raghubir Singh. On appeal by Raghubir Singh the Revenue Appellate Authority set aside the order of the SubDivisional Officer on March 6, 1973 and remanded the case to the Sub Deputy Officer, Hanumangarh, for fresh determination of the call area for grant of land for Raghubir singh. The matter was taken to the Board and by its order dated 14th April, 1975 directed that the ceiling areas for RaghubirSingh may be determined according to old law i.e. Act of 1955 and not according to the new law i,e.Act of 1955. In pursuance of the direction of the Board, the Sub- Divisional Officer, Bikaner held that Surendrapal Singh (appellant) aged 12 years was a minor daughter of Raghubir singh and used to 725 study in Punjab and further held that the land in possession of RaghubirSingh was ancestral. Aggrieved by the order dated May 6, 1976 passed by the Board the Sub Sub Divisional officer filed revision application before the Board for Rajasthan. The Board of revenue dismissed the same and upheld the order. The appellant preferred a writ petition before the High Court which allowed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of Raghubir SINGH that no appeal having been filed by the State from the order the Sub Division Officer dated 5th April 1976, the said order became final and the board of Revenue had no jurisdiction to set aside that part of the order which had gone against the State and in his favour. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that it was not correct to say that Section 9 is limited to the executive control and superintendence of the Boards over subordinate revenue courts and it does not apply to judicial proceedings. [766C] 2.1 In the Government of India Act of 1935 there was provision under Section 224 for superintendence by the High Courts ', but subsection(2) made it clear that this superintendence would not be construed as giving to the High court any jurisdiction to question any judgment of any inferior court which was not otherwise subject to appeal or revision. [765D] 2:2 The Board has power over all revenue courts. In view of the language of Section 221 of the Act of 1956, it is clear that the Board 's powers of superintendence and control over all Revenue Courts are similar to those conferred by Section 9 of the Land Revenue Act, 1915. [76F G] 3.1 The Board had by its orders dated 14 th April, 1976 directed that "the ceiling area may be fixed according to new law" i. e. Act No. 1 of 1955 & not according as to the old law. [77G H] 2 :3 In the instant case also the High ' Court did not go into the merits of the controversy nor did it advisable to into it and it would be for the Sub Assistant Officer, who committed the grave illegality on not merely ignoring the law but also ignored the directions of the board itself. It is clear from the language used in Section 221 that the Chairman of the State Board has general powers of supervision and control of all revenue Courts. In this case also, the High "Court" had by the impugned order dated 4th April 1975 directed the Sub Collector to decide the matter in the light of the observations of theBoard. It was not necessary for the Board to exercise its powers of judicial superintendence and it could not, therefore, make use of its powers under Section 9.

The appellant, a newspaper employee of the respondent State, was engaged in the production or distribution of newspapers and news materials. The Central Government issued an order on the basis of recommendations of Justice Palekar. The appellant challenged the validity of the said order by filing writ petition in the High Court which allowed the same holding that the law reports were not newspapers within the meaning of section 2(b) of the Act and therefore the demand made by the Deputy Labour Commissioner to comply with the order made by it on the ground of publication of the newspaper reports was unsustainable by its judgment dated 22nd April, 1983. The High Court accepted the plea of the Ist respondent and declared that the Law Reports were not newspaper within the ambit of section 1(b). Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: (1) The law reports published by the Ist Respondent are newspapers and the employees employed by the appellant in their production or publication of these public news reports should be extended the benefit of the orders passed by the Central Government on the recommendation made by Justice P.alekar Award. [782G H] (2) The expression `newspaper ' as defined in the Act includes not merely `public news ' but also `comments on public news and information. The Act in question is a beneficent legislation which is enacted for the purpose of improving the conditions of service of the employees of the newspapers establishments and hence even if it is possible to have two opinions on the construction of the provisions of the statute the one which advances the object of the enactment and is in favour of the employee for whose benefit the Act is passed has to be accepted. [788B] (3) The word `new ' as used in section 2 (b) includes not only `public newspaper but also every other person employed to do any work in, or in relation to, any newspaper establishment. It is significant that the expression `public News ' is defined by section 2 of the Working Journalists (Conditions of Service) and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1955. The definition of `new' as defined under the Act means any printed periodical work containing public news or comments on public News and includes such other class of printed periodicals as may be notified in this behalf by the State Government in the Official Gazette. [789A B] (4) The expressions `public newspapers ' and 'public news reports ' are not defined in section 1 (b). They are, therefore, matters in which the public is interested. [783C D] (5) The definition includes not mere `public publication ' but `comment on public newspaper. [784E F] (6) The words `new or periodical work ' as understood in the dictionary meaning of `public media ' and `public information ' are used in the sense that they are intended to be used for the purposes of improving their conditions of services. [779D E] (7) The term `new" is defined in Section 2(c) of Act as any working journalist, and includes any other person engaged to do or do any business in, any news establishment. [781E F]. (8) The publication of a newspaper ' as contemplated by section 1 of the Press and Registration of Books Act, 1867, by itself may not be sufficient to make a law report a newspaper which may after some time cease to be a newspaper and become a book of reference.

The appellant was a licensee of the respondent. The agreement was described as an agreement of 'leave and licence ' entered into between the respondent on the one hand and the appellant on the other wherein the respondent had been described as the licensee and the recitals therein recite that the licensor was seized and possessed of and was otherwise well entitled as the monthly tenant of the workshop premises situated at 231, Ripon Road, Cooperative Building, Bombay. The licence was to commence from 1st September, 1965 to 31st August, 1970 and it was further submitted that the licensee had approached the licensor to allow him to occupy and use the said premises for the purpose of carrying out his business of workshop for a period of five years and whereas the licensor had agreed to allow the licensee to use the premises under the leave and licence of the licensor for a term of five year. The respondent filed an application for eviction on the ground that he was in occupation of the premises on 1st February, 1973 under a subsisting agreement for licence. The Small Cause Court held that the appellant was not a sub tenant but a licensee and not a tenant. The High Court allowed the revision on the view that there was no subsisting agreement between the parties and that the respondent was a tenant and having found that the period of licence had come to an end, he passed an order of eviction against the appellant. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1.1 In view of the intention of the parties in the document and the facts and circumstances of this case it is a licence and not an agreement. good deal of submission was made before us that if it was a lease and not as a lease, then this point could be taken in aid of the submission that the Court had to jurisdiction, and there was nothing on record to show that after 31st March, 1966 the leave & licence agreement between parties was renewed or any fresh agreement was entered into. The appellant 's contention that it was an agreement for leave and Licence was not supported by any evidence. good dealing of submission is made before this Court that if the exclusive possession to which a person was entitled under an agreement with a landlord was coupled with an interest in the property, the agreement would be construed not as mere licence but as a licence. good dealt of submissions were made before it that if there was any error apparent on the face of the record, the error if any has to be discovered by long process of reasoning, and the High Court should not exercise jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution. [231B C] 1.2 In view the background of the entire document evidencing the contention of the appellant that it is an agreement to leave and license, good deal o submission was submitted before this court that if this point had been taken in support of the plea that there were no subsisting contract for licence on the 1st of February 1973 as there was none on record, then the point could not be taken aid of. [232D] 1:3 In view Of the facts of this appeal and the background and the circumstances of the whole document evidencing its contention that the lease was not put an end to by the appellant and that in any event by filing the application for ejectment the appellant licensor had granted an implied licence to the respondent licensee to continue in possession till a decree of eviction was passed in his favour. This decision was remanded back to the High court and it is directed that the appeal be heard afresh in accordance with law because in a previous decision Vaidya, J. by the judgment dated 9th December, 1975 as mentioned hereinbefore had allowed the appellant ' s appeal.

The appellant company was incorporated in the State of Rajasthan. The Ruler of the Jodhpur State merged with the State Government and became a part of the covenanting State till such time as they were modified by the new State. On January 26, 1950, the Ruler of Jodhpur State transferred his rights to the Company under article 295(2) of the Constitution. In pursuance of this agreement the appellant company transferred its rights in favour of the Company on August 1, 1951 and on February 2, 1952, the Company was merged with it by virtue of the provisions of the Covenant. The Company continued to be a part B State of Madhya Pradesh till January 26. 1950. On March 12, 1952 the Ruler issued a notification under article 296(2), which provided that all the existing laws in the covenanted State shall continue until they were repealed or altered and the liabilities arising from the existence of those laws shall be the assets and liabilities of the Union. The appellant company filed a writ petition in the High Court for quashing the said notification on the ground that it was not in dispute that on January 26 1950, there was no recognition of the liability by the old State of Dholpur to; refund the amount of tax collected in advance for no export was made and that the liability did not devolve on the Part B State. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that article VI could not be enforced by citizens against the new sovereign as it emerged on January 1, 1950. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The agreement was not a law. It was part of an agreement between the Ruler and the Ruler. [184 D] (2) The covenant in the agreement was only a recognition of rights of subjects and that there was always recognition by the Union of India as regards the liabilities of all old States which eventually were included in it subject always to this that if the new law is within the competence of the State legislature and does not transgress the constitutional limitations after the Constitution came into force.

The appellants were the sellers of certain agricultural crops in the State of Madras. The appellants were not prevented from doing their business, for they could still utilise it for commodities other than the notified crops. The State Government considered them and declared the areas to be specified in the notification or any portion thereof to be a notified area for the purpose of the Act. The appellant contended that the appellants had really two fundamental rights: one was to carry on trade or business and the other was to hold their property, i.e., the market; that by reason of the notification they were not prohibited from holding the market as property, for them could still utilize it for commodity other than notified crops; and that the appellant had no right to do business in the market established subject to the regulations and also did business outside the prescribed area ; and that they were therefore not prohibited by bye laws framed under the Act, and that there was no violation of article 14 of the Constitution. Held, that the scheme of the bye law prohibiting the deduction of trade allowance and does not operate upon any other payments made which are not trade allowances. The object of the statute is to ensure that the market committee complies with the requirements of the law and it is not open to the Government to fix a long distance as a prohibited area; and so too, A, the seller may purport to sell one maund of cotton but in fact deduct a small part of it, retain that part for himself or give it to C. The question whether 'mahimai ' is a trade allowance depends upon the nature of that deduction. If on the other hand, mahimai ' was a deduction out of the price or commodity agreed to be paid or transferred, it would not be a deduction from the price and commodity within the meaning of section 14 of The Act.

The appellant was convicted by the Sessions Judge under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C., and sentenced to death on the ground that he had committed the murder of his wife. The High Court confirmed the sentence but reduced the sentences to transportation for life. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the High Court should have imposed a sentence of transportation for the offence of murder on the appellant and that the sentence should be reduced to transportation. HELD : (i) The High Courts were right in reducing the sentences of death to transportation in these two cases mainly because of the difference of opinion between the High Courts, not only on the question of guilt but also on the point of sentence. [426 B] (ii) The fact that the appellant was a young man and had no hand in the killing, and there was evidence that he did not give him any name would not make him guilty and so should be acquitted. [413 C D] (iii) The sentence of death imposed on the appel lant was excessive and it was not necessary to impose the lesser penalty. [414 E F] (iv) The appellant had been convicted by a Sessions Judge for murder on his own, but he did no more than inflict a comparatively light head injury. There was evidence to show that there was enmity between the accused and the deceased. It is true that the prosecution case was that the appellants were also there but it was difficult to believe that they would have joined in the attack and so had the actual murder been committed. But what the High court did was to reduce the sentences. [416 C D, F G] (v) The circumstances showed that the two accused were not present at the scene of the crime but were only a young brother and the tenant of the appellant in question. There is no reason why the sentence of imprisonment should be enhanced.

The petitioner was appointed as officiating Executive Engineer in Class I service under the Ministry of Works and Housing in Government of India and was compulsorily retired by order dated 3.8.1976 with effect from 5.11.1976 made under Rule 56(j)(i) after he had attained the age of 50 years. The petitioner challenged that order for retirement and has claimed payment of remuneration which he would have been entitled to draw upto the normal date of superannuation. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Government servant officiating in Class II service or post could be retired compulsorily by exercising the power under Rule56(j) (i) on the ground that he was not in Class 1 or Class II Service or post and had entered Government service before attaining the age Of 50 years; and that the petitioner was entitled to salary and other allowances payable to him from the date of compulsory retirement till the date he completed the age. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the order for retiring the petitioner from Class I Service or Post could not be treated as a Government servant in Class 11 service or posts and that since the petitioner had attained his age of 55 years on 10.2.1972, he should be deemed to have been in Class III service or Class I services or post at the relevant time and that he would be entitled to receive salary and allowances from the dates of compulsory retire ment till the day of his normal superannuation. Dismissing the writ petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The object of Fundamental Rules 56(J) is to confer power on the appropriate authority to compulsorily retire Government servant who in Class ' I or Class ' II service Or post, whether substantively, temporarily or on officiating basis. If the officia tion is not brought to an end by reverting the Government Servant to his substantive post before the power of retirement is exercised, the Government employee con cerned must be taken to be in Class 7 or Class 11 Service or posts at the time and would come within the ambit of sub clause (i). There is, however, no warrant for the conclusion that officiating Government servants in Class 8 or Class 10 service or Post are outside the purview of sub cl.(i) of Rule 56. [638C D] 2. The purpose of Fundamental Rule 56 (j)(ii) is not to confer powers on the competent authority to compulsory retire Government servants who at the first instance, have to go back to the substantive post from which he has been promoted on an officiating basis or on a tempo rary basis and it is obvious that he has no right to the post and can always be reverted to the posts, if any, on which he had a lien. [643E F] 3. The intention of Fundamental rules 56( j) is that Government servant is in Class 10 or Class III Service orpost at the same time as his substantive appointment. If he is only a temporary hand, he has to be taken into Class I or class II service and would bring within the purview Of sub clause(i). [643F G] 4. The scope of Fundamental rule 56(jj) is confined to Government servants serving in Class 9 or Class 9 service on substantive, temporary or offi ciating basis. But if he is merely a temporary employee, he can be reverted back to his original post before he attains the age o n superannuation. [538F] 5. The concept of "if he is in class I orClass II service" is not relevant to the exercise of power contained in F.R. 56(q) of the Fundamental Rules. [525G H] 6. The expression "if a Government Servant belonging to a Class I and Class II services or posts is in such service orpost as covered by sub clause.(i).

The appellant Corporation had taken a loan from the Life Insurance Corporation of India for the purpose of construction of a building. The proposal was accepted by the Divisional Manager on 11th January, 1961 and as such there was no concluded contract between the deceased and the Corporation. On the death of the deceased, the amount covering two cheques were lying in the deposit and in the suspense account of the Corporation and was not adjusted towards the premium since the proposal was not considered, the terms of acceptance were not fixed and the premium amount required for the proposal. The suit was filed by the plaintiffs respondents claiming a decree for Rs. 1,00,000/ with interest at 18% per annum from 11th February, 1961 till payment. The Trial Court held that there was a concluded contract of insurance between the parties and that the deceased was assured and told by the local agent and the field officer of the corporation that the payment of first premium would amount to acceptance of the proposal if the proposal is not accepted, the term of acceptance was not fixed. On appeal, the High Court held against the appellant Corporation. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The proposal sent by the deceased did not indicate the position alleged by the appellants that there were assurance on behalf of the field officers and local agent to the deceased that the payments of first premiums would amount acceptance of proposal if it was not otherwise accepted. [85G] 2.2 The proposal must be accepted by all concerned authorities of the Life insurance Corporation established that the proposal sent through its acceptance letter dated 11th May, 1961 was for some reason 357 or other not accepted by it. [86B] 3.3 In the instant case there was assurance on the part of the respondent that the amount paid would amount towards the acceptance of a proposal. It was also admitted that the cheque issued towards the first premium was encashed and the appellant corporation had encashed the cheques issued towards premium. The High Court was of the view that having regard to the conduct of the parties, there was an assurance on their part that the repayment of the sum would amount only to the acceptance. [87C] 4.4 In the present case there is no evidence that such could have been the deposition in law. There was a clear admission by the respondent Corporation that the cheques were encashed and that it was never appropriated by it in its accounts and the said premium amount 354 was received by the Corporation without any demur or qualification and that in any event the Corporation must be deemed to have waived by its conduct formality, if any, of sending communication of its acceptance of proposals. [88D] 5. The contention that the respondent corporation had accepted the proposal for Rs Learned Trial Judge was correct. It is not disputed that there is a concluded and valid insurance contract between both the parties namely principal together with interest is paid back to the Corporation by the appellantCorporation. [89E] 6. In the facts and circumstances of the case there will be no order as to costs in this Court.

The appellant company was carrying on business in coal and coal. The company had been granted a certificate under section 109 of the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The Company applied for an interim injunction restraining the company from proceeding with its business. The trial court dismissed the application holding that the order granting interim injunction did not determine the rights and obligations of the parties in relation to the matter in dispute in the suit. In appeal the High Court held that the cause of action was personal to the insolvents and did not vest in the assignee, and accordingly set aside the decree and remanded the suit for trial. The appellant company appealed to this Court by special leave. HELD: (i) An order passed by the High court in an appeal which does not finally dispose of a suit or proceeding from which appeal has arisen, is not final within the meaning of article 133(1)(c) since the controversy between the parties when the complaint in respect of offences under sections 467 and 468 read with section 114 I.P. Code was concerned merely with an order passed on by the court of the rights of the party in dispute. If the decision on an issue put an end to the suit, the order will undoubtedly be a final one but if the suit or proceedings were a live one yet to be tried, the decree is interlocutory. [934 C D] (ii) The expression "final order" in article 133 (1)(b) means an order which finally determines the points in dispute and brings the case to an end. If it did not, and the suit was still left alive and has got to be proceeded in the ordinary way no finality could attach to the order. [1034 C] (iii) The High Court was right in holding that an order by the trial court dismissing the application for interim injunction was not a final order within the ambit of article 134(1) (c) because the controversy involved between the two parties when they were the same, and it was not contended that the decision of the High Courts amounted to a judgment or decree.

The respondent company was manufacturing grey cloth in the hands of the processor. The processed fabric was sold by the processor to the processor on payment of excise duty at the factory gate. The processor 's factory was assessed to excise duty under Item No.2(a) of the First Schedule to the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985. The respondent company filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the assessment order contending that the assessable value of the processed fabric would be the value of grey cloth plus the value thereof and manufacturing expenses which would be either included in the price at which he would be selling the processed goods in the market, that would be taken by the Excise authorities as the assessable values of the grey cloth or manufac turing profit and expenses; that the valuation of the fabric would not be the price for processing the fabrics; that there was no justification for the respondent company to charge any duty on the grey fabrics manufactured by it; that in view of the fact that the processed fabrics were sold by processor, the respondent Company had discharged its liability to pay excise duty on such goods and the value at which they would be sold was Rs.30, being the value as sessable value; that since the processed cloth was sold for processing, the price of grey fabric would have been higher than the assessable price; that even if the processed yarn was sold in the factory, the assessee would not have discharged its liabil ties under Item Nos.2 and 3 of the first Schedule to Central Excise Act, 1944; that as the processed cotton fabric had been sold for the processing of job work, the value would be Rs.20 and the manufacturing expenses would be more than Rs.5 lakhs; that if the grey fabric was not sold by him, then in such a case the value should be Rs.,30, having regard to the fact whether the processed textile fabrics were actually sold or not; that it would be appropriate to include the processor ' sessageable value. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, on behalf of the appellant company it was contended that the market value of processed fabric should be the assessable valuation of processed fabrics and excise duty would be payable at the rate of Rs.60 per kg. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The assessable value would not include the processing charges and costs, expenses and manufacturing profit plus the cost of the job work done plus the manufacturing profit and the expenses. [346B] 2.2 In order to explain the position it is made clear that the declared value at the gate for the processed Fabric would be as per Rule 174 of the Central Excises Rules 1944. The price at Which the grey yarn was subjected to would give a declaration to the manufacturer as to what would be its price at the time when the processing fabric would leave the processor, 's factories plus his profit and expense. That would be, in such cases, the assessablevalue of the fabrics plus the valuation thereof and/or manufacturing expenses. That will be the correct as soresable value and manufacturing expenditure but not any other subsequent profit or expenses. It is necessary to include processor 'Sessable Value. [347C D] 2(a). The expression "deemed factory" in Rule 174 is used in a wide sense, to mean the factory of the manufacturer who entrusts the goods to the processing machine for processing on job work basis. [348F G] (b) In order that the processor may be selling or purchasing the processed articles in the markets, it would include only the price or deemed price at what would he be selling and the said goods must be the cost at which the processed article would give declaration to him as to how would be his sale. [349C] 3(b) The expression 'deemed factory ' is used to mean a factory of manufacturer who entrusted the goods with the processing machinery for processing or processing.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk on June 1, 1963 by the Panchayat Samiti, Loharu. He was confirmed in that post in course of time. On January 21, 1974 he was promoted as a Head Clerk. The Punjab Panchayat Samitis and Zilla Parishads (Haryana Amendment) Act, 1973 introduced extensive amendments in the Act of 1961. Section 33 of the Amending Act provided that persons employed by a Panchayat Samiti before April 1, 1973 and who were in service at the commencement of the amending Act shall continue to be governed on the same terms and conditions on which they were employed by the Panchayats Samiti from time to time. The appellant was confirmed as a head clerk on an ad hoc basis. On March 14, 1975 he was appointed a Head clerk. He continued to work as a full time Head Clerk till June 13, 1973 when the Amending Ordinance came into force. He challenged his absorption on a higher post in the Panchayat Samitis before the High Court of Punjab and Haryana. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant was entitled to continue in the service of the Panchayat even though he had been appointed as head clerk. Allowing the appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 The appointment of the appellant to the post of a Head Clerks prior to his absorption in Government service had to be recognised and protected, despite the fact that such appointment was made after June 13 1973 when Amending Act came into effect. [738C] 1.2 In view of this deletion, the Panchayat Samities were divested of their power to make appointments to the Panchayat. The fact that the appel lant was promoted on an Ad hoc basis in January 1974 or the further fact that he was appointment lawfully to the posts of a head Clerk prior to the amendment came into operation on June 13. 1973 when amending Act came in force, cannot improve his position for the simple reason that these appointments were made after July 13,1973 when the Amendment Act came to be passed. [750D E] 1:3. The appointment was not made after the date on which the Panchayat had lost its power to making appointments to Panchayat. It could not, therefore, have appointed the appellant as a Sub Clerk in any event.

The appellants filed a suit claiming that the property in dispute belonged to the Math Sauna or the deity and that Mahant Shivshankar Yati was in possession thereof as Mahant and Sarbarakar of the deity. The suit was decreed by the Civil Judge, Ghazipur in respect of the two fixed deposits made by Mahant Shiv Shankar Yati and Mahant Shivpher Yati. In appeal, the High Court held that Sadashiv Yati had not been a regularly constituted Mahant of Math Saauna and Sarbakar of temple and that Sadasiv Yatti was not a regularly appointed Mahant of the temple and consequently, the Amauli properties must be regarded as his personal property and they did not belong to the institution or deity. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the income from the property was purchased by Mahant Ram Shivshanker Yati in 1921 from 662 the personal and separate funds inherited by him from his predecessor Shivphej Yati; (ii) the Amaul properties were described by Mahant SHIVshankar Yadav as properties of the Math and therefore a claim to exemption from levy was made. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The fund from which the Amaiuli properties were acquired constituted the personal property of Mahant Shivsh Shankar Yatri and do not form part of the properties of Math or the temple; (iii) the liability of the Mahant Shiv Shanker Yati to tax was on the person who makes the claim. [657C D] 2. The High Court has found that the claim was not accepted by the assessing authority, and that the position in regard to those properties taken in the assessment proceedings was adopted by the Mahant only for the purpose of escaping personal liability to tax. In the result, the appeal is dismissed with costs.

The appellants were displaced persons from West Pakistan. They filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution in the High Court challenging the validity of the notification issued thereunder on March 24, 1955. The High Court dismissed the petition and held that the jurisdiction to revise the order had been taken away by virtue of the provisions of section 12(2) and 19 of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the power of the Custodian under the , to allot any property to a person or to cancel an allotment made in favour of a person rests on the fact that the property vests in him. HELD: (1) The expression "any property" is not defined in section 2(a) of the , and it includes all properties which are held by the Custodian as his own. [6C D] (2) The definition of evacuee property in section 3(a)(i) of Act, does not include any property which is held or acquired by a person whether such allotment or lease was granted before or after the commencement of the . [6D E] (3) The word "property" in section 4(a), means all properties and rights which are vested in the Custodian. It includes all lands which are evacuee property. [7E H] (4) The words "any person" in clause (i) to (iii) of section 3 of the, include any person who is a displaced person. [8G H] In the instant case, the Custodian by reason of the divesting of the property as from March 24 1955 had become functus officio with respect to it and could not rectify any error made by him in the past in the matter of cancellation of allotment. Sub section (2), therefore, cannot be said that section 19(1) of The Act is completely in conflict with section 10 of the in so far as the question of cancellation is concerned. [9E F] (5) The Custodian has no jurisdiction to cancel a allotment or leases made in his favour. [10G H; 11A] (6) The notification under section 12 of the with respect of any property or class of property would cease to be evacuee property, the displaced person to whom land was allotted "held" the land and was in possession of such property at the date of the publication of the Notification under section 13(1). [11B C] (7) The power of a managing officer or a managing corporation is in conflict With section 10 Of the Act, it permits cancellation only on certain specified grounds and, therefore, it cannot be held that section 18 is completely inconsistent with section 19 of 1954 Act.

The Uttar Pradesh Public Service Commission invited applications from eligible candidates for recruitment to the post of Upper Zila Basic Shiksha Adhikari (Women), District Inspectress of Girls Schools/Associate Regional Controllers of Girls School in Uttar Pradesh Educational Service Junior Scale (Care) and DistrictHOK of Girls schools/Associates Regional Controllers, in Uttar pradesh. The advertisement inviting applications from qualified candidates was published on May 5, 1985 and a corrigendum was published by the State Government on June 8, 1985. The recruitment examination was in two stages written and interview/personality test. After the written examina tion was over, on the basis of the results thereof success ful candidates upto a base limit have to be called to be interviewed. On account of improper feeding into the comput er some of the candidates who had better performance in the written examination were not called and candidates securing lesser marks in the viva voce were not only called for interview but were also finally selected. When this position was known and upon an inquiry was factually estab lished, the Public Service Com mission cancelled the entire recruitment examination and asked for a fresh interview of all eligible candidates on the ground that they had better performances in the selection process. The High Court upheld the action of the Public Services Commission and dismissed the writ petitions. Hence these appeals by special leave. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 When no defect was pointed out in regard to the written test and the sole objection was confined to exclusion of a group of successful candidates in the oral examination from the interview, there was no justification for cancelling the written part of the recruitment examina tions. [125B] 1.2 The situation could have been appropriately met by setting aside the recruitment and asking for a new interview of the two Scheduled Caste candidates and five Backward Class candidates has become final and would not be disturbed. The State Public Service commission should have been more careful in dealing with the matter so that four years in the process of recruitment would not have been lost and the public cause would not hail if the litigation could have reached. [126C D] 1:3 In the instant case, when no defect had been pointed out by the appellant, the High Court has upheld the actions of the public Service Commission and has dismissed the Writ Petitions. The selection of two Scheduled Castes candidates and 5 Backward Class candidate has become complete and would be in accordance with the interview part of recruitment and on the principle of equality of opportunity enshrined in Article 14 of the Constitution. [127F G] 1 :4 In the process, there is hardly any justification for cancellation of the written parts of the selection examina ble. The procedure adopted by the Public Commission has been completely misconceived and has resulted in violation of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitu tion. [128B C] 2.1 The situation can have been suitably met by set aside the selection and asking the for a second interview of only eligible candidates in accordance wit h the written and the freshly held interview became eligible for selection. There is no justification to cancel the written Part of the Recruitment Examination and asking a fresh examination of all other eligible candidates. [129C D, E] 2:2 The State Government should have be more careful while dealing with matters so that 4 years in process of selection would not has been lost.

The appellant, a mahant of the Dera at Landeke was an independent Dera and that he had no right to recover possession of the properties. The suit was filed on the basis that the appellant as the lawfully appointed mahant was entitled to manage the properties of the dera at landeke. The trial court held that the plaintiff had failed to bring on record the legal representatives of the deceased, that the defendant was unlawfully claiming to be the mahant and that the appeal could be continued under Q. 10(1) (a). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the suit was barred by limitation because the appellant had no knowledge about the date of death of Som Dass and that there was no certainty as to the person who would become the mahants of Dera after the death of the Som Dass. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The rule is based on the principle that trial of a suit cannot be brought to an end merely because the interest of a party in the subject matter of the suit has devolved upon another during the pendency of the litigation but that suit may be continued against the person acquiring the interest with leave of the Court. [912 E] 2. The fact that it was after Som Dass died that Shiam Dass was elected to be a mahants and as it was in the same representative capacity that the application was sought to be continued, that he was lawfully appointed Mahant of Dia after the deceased had expired. [1013 B] 3. The appellant could not be added as parties under Order 22, rule 10 notwithstanding that the period of limitation for impleading them had elapsed. [1113 C] 4. The position that it is after Som Chand died that he became the maties of the Sectinion and when a dispute was raised about such rights then the appellant was bound to bring the legal representative of the former mahant later on died during the course of the trial but that decree could be continue against the successor in interest with the leave of this Court. The High Court should not have granted leave to the appellant to prosecute the appeal. [1213 D] 5. In the instant case, the suit had abated and dismissed the suit. [1413 E] 6. The question whether the devolution takes place as a consequence of death or for any other reason is decided by this Court in Roshan Lal vs Kapur Chand, that it would be applicable if the devolution took place when Shiam Das was elected as mahant after the date on which the death had occurred and, therefore, Order 22 rule 10 will apply. [1513 E F] 7. The appeal could not have been dismissed on the ground of limitation because it was filed beyond time prescribed by law. [1614 B] 8. In Roshan Lal (supra) this Court took the view that devolution of interest in the land is a matter of succession and, as such, Order 21 rule 10 would apply. It was not necessary for the appellant under Order22, rule 3 to bring to an appropriate end merely if the interests of a person in the property had devolved upon him by virtue of law 490 or custom that there would be devolution of the interest in that subject matter. [1715 E] 9. The facts of the present case are similar to those in Roshanlal Lal vs Kapoor Chand, and it was not possible for this Court to have granted any leave to appeal against the decree of the court below. [1816 D] 10.

The petitioners, who were Government employees in the State of Andhra Pradesh, were appointed as Assistant Engineers in the Public Works Department on different dates between January 1, 1979 and October 29, 1979. The age of retirement was increased from 55 to 58 years by a notification dated October 29.8.1979. The petitioners challenged the reduction of their age of superannuation from 58 to 55. The Government of Andhra State issued a notification on September 17, 19,975 fixing the age of the employees as 55 and directing that the age should be increased from 58 years to 60. The State Government by its order dated October 16, 1979 fixed the age for retirement of all Government employees, other than in the last Grade Service, from 58 upto 58 years. The petitioner challenged the said notification on the ground that it was unreasonable. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the reduction was not arbitrary or unreasonable in the circumstances of the case. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the petitioners that the Government had acted unreasonably in not giving any previous notice to the employees which would have enabled them to arrange their affairs on the eve of retirement; that the State Government had exercised its power arbitrarily without having regard to factors which are relevant on the fixation of the age and, therefore, the decision taken by the Government was bad for a total non application of mind to the relevant facts and circumstances bearing on the question of the date of retirement. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The proviso to Article 309 read with Article 313 of the Constitution is not violative of Article 14 or Article 16 since it is not arbitrary nor unreasonable in its circumstances. [723D] 2.1 The Government had taken a decision on its own to increase the age from 55 and 58 years, that the said recommendation was accepted by the State government and consequently, the age was raised to 58 with effect from October 29 l 979. It is not therefore arbitrary or irrational in the facts of the present case. No. The contention of the petitioners is that the proviso which conferred a benefit upon Government servants by protecting their conditions of service, cannot be amended so as to empower the Government to alter those conditions to their prejudice and, in any event, they cannot be changed retrospectively so as not to take away rights which had already accrued to them. [758E F] 2:2 The Government was therefore justified in its contention that arbitrary fixation of retirement age amounts to "removal" from service and is therefore violative of article 14 or 16 since the employees had acted on the representation made to them in 1979 by increasing the age Of retirement from 55 years to 58; that as a result of the increase in the age, of retirement from 58, to 55, the vested right had accrued to the petitioners, which could be taken away, if at all, only from future entrants to the Government service; and that the decision of the Government is bad for any total non Application of mind. [759E F G] 2 :3 The Government has acted unreasonably without giving any prior notice to employees who had already been stagnated in the lower positions due to expansion of educational facilities; that, the present measure was intended to have a salutary effect on the creation of incentives to the deserving employees whose number was increasing enormously due to increase in age of Retirement from 55to 58 years; that it would take welfare measures in order to improve the lot of the common man, and. particularly, in orderto afford opportunities to qualified and talented unemployed youths whose number is increasing enormally due to increased expansion of education from 55 To 58; and, the Government employees were stagnated by the increase of the ages of retirement, which was due to the increase being caused by expansion of Educational facilities; and the present action was intended for reducing the age.

The appellants were dealers in the State of Haryana. They were assessed to sales tax under section 5(1) of the Punjab Sales Tax Act, 1973 on the purchase of raw materials from outside the State and used them in the manufacture of goods specified in Schedule B. The assessing authority levied a tax on the purchases effected by the appellants on the ground that they had purchased raw materials for the purpose of export within the meaning of section 5 (1) (b) of Act 20 of 1973. The appellants challenged the levy of tax on these purchases and contended that the transactions were not taxable under section 9(1)(b) as they were not sales in the course of inter State trade or commerce in the territory of India within the definition of 'turnover ' in section 5 of the Central Sales Tax, 1956. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the purchases of raw material by the assessees were not charge able to tax either under section 3(1), or section 6 or section 24(3). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the words "disposes of" used in clause (a)(ii) later, clause (b), should be deemed to have been deleted from the statute. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The expression "disposition of goods liable to tax under Section 9" in section 9 (1)(c) must be deemed not to have used the goods for the purposes speci fied therein i.e. for the manufacture or sale of any other goods and dispose of the manufactured goods in any manner otherwise than by way of sale in the inter State or in the Course of export out of the territory within the term of sub section (1). [351C D] 2. The words "or despatches the manufactured materials to a place outside the state" in clause(a)(i) later inserted with retrospective effect from 27.5.1971, which included cases where the purchase tax is payable under any other provision of this Act, there shall be levied, subject to the provisions of section 17, a tax at such rate as may be notified under section 15. [351D] 3. The appellant was the owner of certain goods. The goods were exported by the appellant to Bombay and the goods were delivered to the sellers on their shipment. The sales tax authorities held that the goods remained the sellers ' property till they crossed the customs barrier and thus entered the export stream, and therefore no tax was realisable on these sales in view of the provisions of article 286(1)(b) of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the words " a person" in section 10(b) were not intended to be used in the sense that the property was intended to pass and did pass on the shipment of the goods. Held, that the word " a registered dealer" in article 286 (1)(a) means " a Registered dealer to whom he sells the goods". The words " only a registered dealers" are not meant to be understood in the ordinary sense of the term. It is well settled that where a person has given such certificate under section 8(b), he has the intention as stated and ultimately he sells to a person who is not a registereddealer for despatch of the consignment outside the State of Bombay, the purchasing dealer may not be liable for having made a false declaration. The words ' only a registration dealer ' are used in different senses and they are capable of being construed in their ordinary sense. In the present case the goods did not pass to the buyers on shipment but were despatched by the sellers to the appellant or by a registered registered dealer to which he sold the goods to an address outside the state of Bombay within a period of six months from the date of purchase by the dealer furnishing such certificate. The mere fact that the sales were on FOB contracts property in the goods passed to the buyer at some point of time before shipment, that is, after they had crossed the Customs barrier and therefore the sales must be held to have taken place "in the course of export" and the exemption under article 286 was not available to the purchasing dealers. The word " registered dealer ' has been defined in section 2(b)(i) as including a person whose business is carried on by him or by his agent, and includes a registered manufacturer. In order that the definition may be given in the context of the export trade, it must be shown that the person who has given the certificate under s. 8(a) is a registered trader to whom the goods have sold the articles. The fact that he sells them to a registered consumer does not make him liable for any tax. The expression " a dealer" is used in section 5(b). It means a registered or unregistered dealer to whose business the goods are entrusted and includes an agent, a registered trade association or a person engaged in the business of supplying goods. In other words, the word 'registered ' has not been defined either in the Act or in the Rules framed thereunder. The definition of "registered" is wide enough to include a person carrying on business as a dealer. It means that the expression "registered dealer" means a person registered under section 3(1) of Bombay Sales Tax Act, 1947 and includes any person who carries on business in goods other than those mentioned in the Schedule. In this connection it may be said that if at the time a declaration of intention is made in the certificate the purchasing manufacturer has the knowledge as stated, and ultimately the seller sells to him a person whom he sold them but who is neither a registered owner nor a registered vendor, the certificate has not not been complied with.

The appellant, who was a married woman, filed an application under section 125 of the Criminal Procedure Code 1973 for a monthly allowance for maintenance. The Magistrate found that the appellant had transferred the suit premises to the respondent and also the shares of the Cooperative Housing Society which built the flat concerned. The appellant 's appeal against the order of the Magistrate was dismissed by the Sessions Judge. In an appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Courts below had overlooked the plain provision in the Explanation (b) to section 125(1) of the Code and that there must be proof of neglect to maintain to attract s.125 and his third contention was that there should be proof that the respondent was a divorcee within the cognisance of that provision. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The main purpose of the payment under any customary or personal law is to avoid destitution of the divorcee and to provide her with wherewithal to maintain herself. [81 C] 2. The object of the Payment of mehar money, as a customary discharge, is to ensure that the wife does not get remarried. The whole scheme of section 127(3)(b) is manifestly to recognise the substitute maintenance arrangement by lump sum payment organised by the custom of the community or the personal law of the parties. [82 D] 3. The purpose of payment under a customary or Personal Law must be to obviate destitution, of the Divorcee and the obligor, not pro tanto but wholly. The intention of the legislature is clear that every divorce otherwise eligible for the benefit of maintenance should be made out if the hurdle of section 125 (4) is to be over come. [83 E] 4. The expression "withal" in the proviso to s. 125(3) of Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 has no application where the husband, by customary payment at the time of divorce, has adequately provided for the divorce, a subsequent series of recurrent does is contra indicated and the husband liberated. [84 E] 5. The conclusion that the liability to pay maintenance had ceased on account of the payments of the sum stipulated by customary or family law whose quantum is more or less sufficient to do duty for maintenance allowance is correct.

The appellant, a tenant in respect of the premises covered by exhibit P 1, leased out to the respondent under exhibit P1.
