The Rent Controller passed an order determining the fair rent at Rs.994 p.m. The appellant 's appeal before the Appellate Authority was dismissed by the Rent Control Tribunal, which held that the building on the land leased under exhibit A1 had also been conveyed to the LIC and that the LIC was entitled to seek fixation of fair rent in respect thereof and that, therefore, the claim in the suit for arrear of rent was barred by section 12(4) of the Act. The High Court dismissed the appeal filed by the appellant. In this appeal it was contended on behalf of the tenants that since the subject matter of the lease was only a vacant piece of land with no title to the buildings standing on the site in item 17 (2), it was not open to the High Court to entertain a collateral attack on the validity or correctness of the order of the Rent Controller. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The question whether the landlord is a tenant or not depends upon the true nature and scope of the jurisdiction conferred on the Rent controller under the Act and, therefore,. impliedly excluded from the purview of the civil court 's jurisdiction as well as the provisions of the . [534B C] 2.1 In the instant case, the question whether a landlord or a tenant is a ryot or not has to be determined by the rent tribunals as a collateral issue in deciding certain applications before them. The fact that an application for this purpose cannot lie except at the instance of a landlord and a tenant, the Rent Tribunal has to deal with this incidentally but this incidentally does not mean that the decision on the question is only the determination as to the fair or standard rent for the premises. [535C D] 2(a) The jurisdiction of the Civil Court is excluded from consideration by the courts as a substantive issue in determining what the fair Rent of the property should be in accordance with the provisions Of the Act, and that even if this relationship exists between the parties, the court of Small Causes will have to deal this incidentally. [635D E] 2.(b) The question on which the jurisdiction of civil court is excluded is only a determination as a final order that is null and void merely because one is valid until set aside, the answer has to turn on the true scope and scope Of the jurisdiction. [553E F] 3(c) In an application under section 4, the jurisdiction is excluded not merely because the question may have had to be considered by theRent Controller but that is not one of the direct issues before the Rent Controllers.

The petitioner was given a provisional seniority list on an integrated seniority list, a position to which he objected. He was also given an opportunity to object to the provi sional list before the final list was prepared. The respondents were not heard after the final lists were published. They filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the provisional list. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the petitioner was entitled to an opportunity of making a representation with regard to the two points urged by him before the Court on the merits and demerits of the case. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the respondents were entitled to a hearing before the provisional seniority lists were still to be prepared after hearing objections, and that the writ petitions should not be entertained as the final seniority list had already been published. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The principle recognised in Shankariah 's case (supra) is not applicable to such a case. [623B] 1.2 The petitioner respondent was entitled only to an ad hoc or temporary appointment and that he should have a further opportunity against even a final seniority lists. If the Central Government had acted properly according to the provisions of the Act, we are of the view that a Court cannot go into the merits or otherwise of equation of posts which is a matter within the province of the Courts to lay down what are in the principles to be adopted for purposes of equation. [723C] 1:3 The petitioner was not entitled to any opportunity against the final gradation list on some such grounds of invalidity, those grounds have to be shown to exist. If he was to have that opportunity the list would not really be final but only provisional or preliminary. Roy 's Case (supra), the opportunity afforded was to be given before the publication of the final select list. [761D] 1 :4 The petitioner had no further opportunity, and it could not possibly be said that he did not have a second opportunity against him. If a particular decision is mala fide or arrived at on totally irrelevant and extraneous consideration ations, such a decision can be interfered with by Courts. [763F] 2.5 In the instant case, the petitioner respondent Dr. R.D. Nanjiah was not able to make out any ground for interference with the final order of the High court. [762B] 3. The petition was dismissed on the ground that it was premature as the provisional gradation list had been still to remain in force. [764C] 4.1 In view of the special circumstances of the present case, there is no merit in this appeal and the same is accordingly dismissed.

The petitioners in both the writ petitions are partnership firms carrying on business of import of rough diamonds and export of cut and polished diamonds. The petitioners in these two writ petitions were granted Additional licences to Export Houses under the Additional Licences category as per para 176 of Import Policy for the period 1978 79 excluding those items which were banner in the policy for the periods 1978 79 and those which have been specifically banned in the prevailing Import Policy, 1985 88. The respondents in both these writ petitions had imported rough diamond and export goods of cut & polished rough diamond. The Additional licences issued to them were valid for a period of 12 months and they contained the following endorsement: "This licence in valid for import of items permissible to Export House under the Import & Export Policy 1988 91 excluding those articles which havebeen specifically banned under the Export Policy,1985 88, pursuant to and subject to the decision of the Supreme Court dated 5.3.1986 in M/s. Rajnikant Brothers case (supra) and had been specifically exempted from the provisions of Import & Exports Policy 1978 89, pursuant thereto and subject thereto the decision on the issue of Additional licences under the import & Export policy 1988 91 was quite different from those contained in the Import and Export Policy for 1978 79. The petitioner in both writ petitions is a partnership firm carrying on trade business of export of rough and polishing diamonds, which were banned in 1977 78. In other words, under the Imports & Exports policy 1988 79 Additional licences are to be given on the basis of one third of the f.o.b. value of the exports made during 1986 87 or earlier periods have been denied the facilities which have already expired in the meantime. The contention of the petitioners is confined to sub para (10) of para 218 of Import and Exports Policy 1988 89 and the Export Houses who were issued Additional licences on or after April 1, 1988, under Import & export Policy 1978 91 are also entitled to a similar relaxation. In the writ petition filed by the respondents it has been contended that under Import and export policy 1988 80 Additional licences were to be granted on the ground of exports made in 1977 79 and that they contained no similarity between the petitioners who have been granted Additional Licences on the date of import and export effected during 1986 88. It is further submitted that under the Foreign Trade Policy 1978 79, Additional licences could be given only on the strength of exports actually made and the value of such Additional licence was only 10 to 12% of the export turnover. The appellants in both cases are also similarly circumstanced as Export Houses which were granted additional licences under Import/ Export Policy 1978 80. In respect of Additional Licences issued to the petitioners, it has further been urged that there is no similarity with the petitioners whose exports have been made during the year 1977 78 and in subsequent years and obtain Additional licences for a much lesser value under the said policy. The learned Additional Solicitor General submitted that there was difference between the conditions for grant of such licences under import & export policy 1978 79 which were quite different and therefore, the petitioners cannot avail the same and are able to import the goods which can be so imported under the prevailing import Policy. In view of the fact that the matter has been pending in this Court and the Additional licences granted to the petitioner have expired in meanwhile we consider it appropriate that the period of validity of the said licences should be extended so that the petitioners can avail the benefit of the same.

The appellant, a manufacturer of excisable goods, was manufacturing the goods. The appellant manufactured the goods in packed condition and the containers were not returnable by the buyer to the assessee. The price of packing materials including those supplied by the appellant was included in the assessable value only when the packing is either manufactured by the assessee or is purchased by the manufacturer or by the supplier to the asses see to the buyer, in respect of all other costs of packing, the cost of such pack ing would have to be added to the price except where the packing was either manufactured at the factory gate or is sold by the purchaser to the purchaser. The Tribunal held that at the time of removal, goods were delivered from the factory in packed conditions and the container was not returnable to by the buyers, there fore, the value had to be included in assessable value. It was further urged that on a correct interpretation of section 4(4)(d)(i) of the Act, the costs of pack ing could be included In the assessable Value only when it is sold at the gate of the factory and not the manufacturer. The contention that the cost price of the drums should be added in the value of the 985 excisable goods was rejected by this Court. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The cost of packing envisaged in section 4 (4)(D)(i), is repugnant to the very scheme of section 3. [520E] 2.1 In cases where the manufacturer supplies the drums and charges the customers separately therefore, under section 4, the Cost of such packing would have been included in that value if necessary, by addition to the sale price, except only where the packaging is durable in nature and is returnable by such buyer to a manufacturer. [620F] 2 2.2 The cost price for which the goods are sold at a factory gate is to be taken as the assessable valuation of the excisable goods. [721B] 3.3 In cases wherein the cost would be included, in the price, the manufacturer levies a charge for the packing which is intrinsically and inevitably incidental to placing the manufactured goods on the market. The cost Of such packaging includes the cost cost of the packing as also the cost thereof. [821C] 4.4 The cost cost envisaged in Section 4(3)(d) does not in clude within its ambit the cost o f packing which was returnable by it to the manufacturer when the packaged is supplied by him to the importer. The manufacturer levies an additional charge for such packing where the price is intrinsally and inevitably ancillary to placing it on the Market. [921F] 4(5)(d). In cases, where the cost is of a durable nature and returnable by t he buyer to his assessee, in all other cases the cost should be included. The "cost of such Packing" referred in section 3 does not mean that while generally the normal price for the sale of the goods is to include cost of packaging which is incidental to putting the excisable article in question, the price of such packages would haveto be added. [1021F G] 4.(6) The cost for packing envisaged under section 3 is repugnant only to the scheme of Section 4. If this question is answered in the affirmative, then in respect o the goods so sold, thecost of the pack ing will have to include in the valuation of such goods where such goods are delivered at the place of removal in packed Condition. [1121F H] 5. The expression "value" in section 2(4) does Not in cluding within its scope mean that in cases where a manufacturer supplies any drums and charge the customers specifically, in terms of sub clause (ii), the cost for such packings shall be included therein.

The appellant was convicted under section 161 I.P.C. and sentenced to undergo R.I. for 15 months under section 5(2) read with section 5 (1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The trial court acquitted him on the ground that there was no independent evidence regarding the demand, the messenger who had contacted PW 1 at the relevant time, had not been examined and the solitary evidence of PW 1 is insufficient, the explanation offered by the appellant was probable and there is no conclusive evi dence to hold that the appellant. The High Court accepted the prosecution evidence, rejected the plea of the appellant and recorded the conviction. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: (1) The presumption arising under section 114 of Evidence Act is not attracted on the proved facts. [337B] (2) The burden resting on the accused person in such a case would not be as light as it is where a presumption is raised under section114 of Evidence Ac tation and cannot be held to be discharged merely by reason of the fact that the explanation tendered by the accused is reasonable and probable. It must further be shown that the explanations are supported by proof, the presumption created by the provision cannot be said to be rebutted. [438C] (3) The onus resting on an accused person under such a cir cumstances would not he as light of it is when a presumption has been raised under Section 114 of the Evidence Act and cannot he held to have been discharged merely because of the facts that the Explanation offered by him is reasonable or probable. [538D] (4) The Court has no choice in the matter, once it is established that the accused persons had received a sum of money which was not due to him as a legal remuneration. It would further be demonstrated that the appli cation of the presumption arises under section 113 of Evidence act and cannot therefore be held t o be discharged simply by reason Of the factthat the explanation offer by the complainant is reasonable, and probable.[538E] (5) The appellant had even by preponderance of probability succeeded in rebutting the presumption.

The respondent company was a public limited company. The company had been in the business of manufacturing and selling various articles of food and drink. It was engaged in the manufacture of food, drink, etc., and was earning income from sale of such articles. For the purpose of its business it was engaged by the company as its own agency. The respondent company had to pay a sum of Rs. 1,50,000/ for the purchase of the said articles. The Company had also to pay an amount of Rs 2,00,000/- for the sale of the articles. In the course of its employment the respondent company paid a sum in cash as advance and the balance of the amount was to be paid by the respondent. The appellant company claimed that it was entitled to recover the said amount from the respondent on account of wrongful withholding of the property of the company. It also claimed that the respondent had been wrongfully withheld from the company for the period from 1st April, 1987 to 31st March, 1988. The trial court held that the appellant company was not entitled to claim any relief under section 630(l)(b) of the Act and dismissed the suit. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had failed to appreciate that the words 'any such property ' in cl. (a) and (b) were referable to existing officers and employees of a company, while cl. On a true construction of the term 'officer or employee ' occurring in sub section (1) of section 630 of H 172 the Act, the scope and effect of the section was limited to such property of a Company which was wrongfully obtained by an officer or employee of the Company during the course o his employment. The beneficent provision contained in section 630 no doubt penal, has been deliberately enacted by the legislature with the object of providing a summary procedure for retrieving the property and thereby giving rise to an obligation to hand over the property back to the company, and observed that the term "officer or employees" used in sub s.(1) was referable to the existing officers or employees of the companies and not to former officers and employee. The High Court of Bombay held that it refers only to the past officers and servants of a public company and not that the phrase 'anysuch property ' used in cl.(a) of sub section(1) meant not only the present officers and Employees but also to include past officers oremployees, and that the expression "any such person" in cl., (b), therefore, did not mean only the past officer and employees but also includes past officers & employees of an company. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The words 'Any such property" used therein must be construed to mean not only a present officer or employees but all that is necessary is that the Court trying the offence has the power to issue a process under sub section.(2) against such officer or servant. [176B] 2. The word "officer" occurring in cl, (a), (b)(i) of Section 630 must be interpreted to mean only past officers, and employees if such officer either (a ) wrongfully obtains possession of any property of that company during the pendency of his employment, to which he is not entitled. [177C D] 3. The expression "officer/ employee" occurring therein in sub sec.(1), means a person who has been placed in possession of property of another company as mentioned in cl (a). It would be rendered nugatory by projecting cl.(b) as applicable to such properties of a companies, possession of which is wrongfully obtained after the termination of his service. [178D] 4.

The appellant was a private Devasthan or a public religious trust. The deity of his worship was Shri Vithal Rukhamai. The founder of the temple had already been succeeded by Guru Govindbuwa and the latter by Balkrishnabuwa, the land had been held in the year 1860 61 in the name of the Devasthan. In the absence of anything to the contrary of a convincing nature, a grant by the Government in favour of the Temple describing the property to be in charge of a manager leads to an unsupport inference that the property is a public temple. The Sanad being an ancient Royal grant was a very important piece of evidence to show that though Sakharam Maharaj, the founder of it had already succeeded by Shri Guru Govind Buwa and his heirs in perpetuity, this land had always been treated as trust property even by the Adhikari saints and the Adhikaris or the disciples who succeeded one after the other were not owners but trustees of the property. The appellant contended that the Sansthan was a public charitable trust within the meaning of section 2(13) of the Act. Held, that when property is dedicated for the worship of a family idol, it is a private and not a public endowment. It is clear from the recitals in the document read as a whole that the dedication to the public or public user of the deity by way of grants from outsiders inconsistent with the private nature of the trust, the nature of devolution of the right, are all important elements in determination of the question whether a property is private or a religious endowment. To sum up from the documentary and oral evidence produced, the following features are present in the present case: (1) The deity installed in the temple was intended by the Founder to be continually worshipped by an indeterminate multitude of the Hindu public; (2) In order to facilitate worship by the public, the Chairman also intended that regular Bhajan, Kirtan and worship shall be conducted by the saintts in succession nominated by the reigning saint.

The assessee was arrested and is being detained in jail in execution of a warrant of arrest issued under section 13 of the Bombay City Land Revenue Act, 1876 for recovery of arrears of land revenue. The Income tax Officer issued the recovery certificate to the Additional Collector of Bombay on the ground that the amount due under a decree had been recovered from him as if it were an arrear of land revenues. The assessee contended that the said amount was not liable to be recovered by reason of the provisions of section 46(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 and that the same offended article 14 of the Constitution. Held, that the contention must fail. The first part of section46(2), which provides for two different modes of recovery of income tax should be framed on a uniform basis, for the recovery of the arrears of revenue, is one and the same, and it is levied under a single Central Act, and yet the ultimate coercive processes for recovery differ in nature and between State and State. The second part of that section provides for different modes to adopt machinery for recovery and the recovery by way of recovery from defaulters of each State, the same mode of recovery, and the third part of the section lays down the procedure for the collection of income taxes. The two methods are equally distinct and separate. The State laws prescribe the procedure in respect of recovery and recovery of tax from defaulters and it can be done easily by suitably amending section 46 (2) so as to provide for the detention of all defaulters for the same period in all cases in all States.

The respondents were the workmen of the Port Trust. The respondents were employed by the Port Board as a casual labourer in the Bombay Port Trust and were paid wages at the rate of Rs. 10 per day for each day. On the question whether the respondents were entitled to overtime work, HELD : (i) The respondents are not entitled to any overtime work. They are not workmen within the meaning of section 2(d)(ii) of the Act. [41 G] (ii) The provisions of section 13 fix the number of hours in a normal working day and not the number specified therein. It is for this reason that a variable recess is in force at the Prince 's and Victoria Docks. The crew at the Alexandra Crew or the crew at a Alexandara Docks get a specified interval of time. [42 E] (iii) The scheme of the rule is to specify that the interval for rest in a working day is given by specifying a day in advance the hours of work in a week. It will also be noticed that the scheme of this rule is not to specify the interval of rest in any particular day. [43 G H] (iv) The rules are to specify a day and work beyond 12 hours. The rule is clear and unambiguous. There is no indication in the rule that the normal working days of work should be so arranged that inclusive of his intervals for rest, if owing to the nature of the work there is difficulty in giving the interval rest. [44 C] (v) The rule does not require that the hours should be worked beyond 12 noon on any particular date. It only means that the hour of work must be so fixed and rest shall not exceed 48.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for ejectment of the respondent tenant on the ground that apart from the controversy about the date which should be the starting point for computing the period of 10 years in view of the language of Sections 39 and 40 of the Act, provisions of this Act will be applicable to the present case. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court allowed the revision petition by holding that since till the matter was pending in the High court 10 years have not been completed and therefore the appellant tenant will be entitled to protection of the provisions of Section 20. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant landlord that as during the pendency of the proceedings in this Court 10 years had elapsed even if the date of completion is taken to be 1.10.86, the appellant would be entitled for the benefit of the provision of Section 2 restriction of the period for 10 years and therefore he will be entitle to protection under the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in holding that if during the proceedings 10 years has elapsed even though the date on which the suit was filed still because of the wording of Sections39 and 40 the appellant is entitled to the benefit under this Act. [167B] 2.1 In order to attract Section 39 the suit must be pending on the date when the commencement of the Rent Control Act, 1947, but in Vineet Kumar 's case (supra) this Court took the view that if at the pendency c.f the litigation even of 10 year have elapsed even then the tenant will not be entitled and therefore it is clear that during the period the tenancy was terminated, the restriction will not apply for 10 1 years and it is thus clear that in Vineet Kr Kumar ' s case (Supra) this court took the same view as in Om 163 Prakash Gupta 's Case wherein it was observed: "Further, in order to invoke Section 39 of the U.P. Act, the suit should be pending at the time of commencement of this act which is 15th of July, 1972 but in our case the protection will be available to the appellant but looking to the language used in Section 39 it appears that the contention advanced by the learned counsel could not be accepted as it was very clear from the language employed in Section39 and it was because of this that in Om163 Prakash Gupta "s case, this Court taken the view in Om 164 Prakash Gupta vs Om 163Prakash Gupta"s case wherein it is clearly held while interpreting Sec. 2 restriction will apply for 9 years and not thereafter. The respondents filed a writ petition in the Lucknow High Court challenging the validity of the revised pay scale. The learned Single Judge allowed the petition holding that the recommendations of the Third Central Pay Commission were not binding on the appellant as no rules had been framed by him for the purpose of entitlement to higher pay scales. The Division Bench also held that the respondents were entitled to get the same scales of pay as was being given in the case of the appellant. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Courts should not have interfered with the recommendations and the rules framed by the Chief Justice of the High 'Court were violative of the constitutional right to equality enshrined in Article 14 of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 The High Courts are under a duty to consider whether the recommendations contained in the Rules are binding on all concerned or not. If the Court has a reasonable nexus with object to being sought for the, as stated under the Rules, the classification made under the rules cannot be said to be violative of Article 14. [298A B] 1:3. The principle is that if the Court had a rational connection with the objects to be taken into consideration, as explained before a particular amount of valuation of the work done by the officers is differ. But the classification has to satisfy two tests: (i) whether there is any element of benefit or not; and (ii) whether the decision is based on an intelligible differentia which distinguishes persons or things that are grouped together from others left out of the group. The appellant was granted a lease of the land to the respondent on July 1, 1945. The lease was for a period exceeding one year and it was not enforceable against the Government. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the lease. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the lease had been granted subsequent to July 1 1945, and that as the lease was only for a limited period, it was neither enforceable against nor illegal under any law in force at the time when the notified date, i.e., July 1 1944, and therefore, the termination of the appellant 's leasehold rights could not be done under the third proviso to section 20(1) of the Abolition Act. The appellants contended that the respondent had created a right in favour of the appellants by virtue of section 20 (2), and that the provisions of sub section (2) of section 18 were not applicable to them, as they did not create any right in any land (whether by way of lease or otherwise) including rights in any forest, mines or minerals, quarries, fisheries or ferries, the transaction was not void. Held: (i) The words " such rights" in the third clause of section 2(1)(a) of Act, are not confined to those rights created before the notified day but only to those right which were created after July 1 1946, and if they are for a duration exceeding one years, they would be valid and enforceable by or against the person in whose favour such right had been created by reason of section 21(1). The words 'such rights' in the second proviso refer to the rights created after the 1st day of July 1945 for a term not exceeding oneyear. [47 D] (ii) The creation of rights after July, 1946, is by the force of the second Proviso itself, void as against the State without any further necessity for any overt act to be done by the Government to avoid the same. If any condition was intended to be super imposed on the right of the Government, it must comply with the conditions laid down in the fourth proviso. [48 E] (iii) The existence of a right created after August 1 1945 is by virtue only of section 3, clause (10), of the Estates Land Act, and not any further need for any positive act to have been done by a landholder on or after July1 1945, if it relates to the private land of the landholder within the meaning of section 4.
